# The Library of Things That Almost Happened

The library appeared on the map only when the rain was heavy enough to blur the street names. It stood between a tailor’s shop and a building that had been a bakery, then a bank, then nothing at all. Its windows were dark, its door was painted green, and a brass plate beside the handle said, simply, LIBRARY. People who noticed it generally assumed it had always been there. People who looked for it a second time usually found a blank wall, or a florist, or an alley too narrow for a building.

Mara found it on the wettest Thursday of October, while carrying a dead fern and a bag of oranges. She had bought the fern three months earlier, after reading that caring for a plant could improve a person’s mood. The fern had responded to her care by turning brown one frond at a time. Now she was taking it to the communal compost bin behind her building, though she was unsure whether the plastic pot could go in as well. The rain began suddenly, and she ducked into the first doorway she saw.

Inside, the air smelled of dust, wool, and something faintly metallic, like a handful of coins. A woman sat behind a desk, repairing the spine of a small blue book. She wore a yellow cardigan and had a pencil tucked through her gray hair. Around her, shelves rose nearly to the ceiling. They were full of books of every size and color, but none had titles on their spines. A ladder leaned against one shelf, and a black cat slept on the reading table, its paws covering its nose.

“We’re open,” the woman said, without looking up.

“I’m only waiting for the rain to stop.”

“That’s what most people come in for.”

Mara placed the fern beside the door. Water dripped from her coat onto a mat embroidered with the words PLEASE TAKE YOUR TIME. She wandered toward the nearest shelf. A book at eye level was bound in red cloth and warm to the touch. She opened it at random. On the page was a short account of a man who had missed his train, met an old friend on the platform, and accepted an invitation to dinner. The friend had served lentil soup. Nothing particularly dramatic followed.

At the bottom of the page, in smaller type, were the words: *The train was six minutes late. The meeting did not occur.*

Mara turned another page. The next account concerned a girl who had found a silver ring in a playground. She had put it in her pocket, taken it home, and spent several afternoons imagining the life of its former owner. Then she had lost it beneath the floorboards. Beneath the account, the same small print explained that the ring had remained buried in the sand until a groundskeeper found it the following spring.

“What are these?” Mara asked.

“Things that almost happened,” said the woman. “Put it back wherever you found it, please. The order matters, though I admit it’s difficult to see how.”

Mara checked the red book’s neighbors before replacing it. “Who writes them?”

“No one, as far as I know. I’m Evelyn.”

“Mara.”

Evelyn nodded as if making a note. “Would you like some tea, Mara? The kettle is already on.”

Mara intended to say no. She had work to finish, wet shoes, and a compost bin to find. But the rain was striking the windows with such conviction that leaving seemed like an argument she would lose. Evelyn made tea in mismatched cups and moved the cat, with evident reluctance, to a chair. They sat at the table. The cat opened one eye, considered them both, and went back to sleep.

“Is this an art project?” Mara asked.

“Not mine, if it is.”

“A research project?”

“I don’t believe so.”

Evelyn spoke without any of the excitement Mara expected from someone making an extraordinary claim. She sounded like a person explaining where the spare light bulbs were kept. Mara asked whether every book described a single almost-event. Evelyn said that some contained hundreds, while others contained only one. The library acquired new books most days, though no one delivered them. Evelyn would arrive in the morning and find one lying on a table or balanced on a shelf, waiting to be cataloged.

“Cataloged by what?” Mara asked.

“By the person who came closest to experiencing it.”

“And how do you know who that is?”

“Usually the book tells me.”

Mara drank her tea. She could have left then, telling herself that Evelyn was eccentric and the books were fiction. Instead, she asked whether there was a book about her. Evelyn regarded her for a moment, not suspiciously but with a kind of practical concern.

“Probably several,” she said. “People often want to read them. They don’t always feel better afterward.”

Mara thought of the fern by the door, the reports waiting in her inbox, and the apartment she had lived in alone for eight months. “I don’t feel especially good now,” she said.

“That does make the question less complicated.” Evelyn opened a drawer, took out a stack of index cards, and began to search.

While she waited, Mara watched rainwater gather at the bottom of the window. Her mother used to say that every choice was a door, but her mother had also bought a bread maker she used twice and kept a cupboard full of unmatched lids. Mara had never thought of her as a reliable philosopher. Since her death, however, ordinary remarks had begun returning with peculiar force. Mara could no longer ask what her mother had meant, or tell her that the fern was dead, or complain about the rain. The absence had made a museum of conversations that had once seemed disposable.

Evelyn found a card and led Mara down a narrow aisle. On the third shelf was a thin green book, its cover worn smooth at the corners. Mara opened it and read about an afternoon when she had almost called her mother. She remembered that day: a crowded bus, a headache, a message from a colleague she had answered instead. In the book, she made the call. Her mother asked whether she was eating enough and described a neighbor’s new dog. They spoke for eleven minutes. At the end, Mara promised to visit on Sunday.

She sat down on the floor to finish the account. Sunday arrived in the book, and she brought pastries. Her mother had bought too many tomatoes. They argued mildly about where to keep them, then ate lunch. There was no revelation, no last-minute warning, no sentence that repaired everything Mara regretted. The afternoon ended with her mother standing at the window, waving as Mara crossed the street.

At the bottom of the final page: *Mara answered the message. She did not call that afternoon.*

She stared at the words until they became shapes. She had been carrying the missed call like evidence of a larger failure, turning it over whenever she couldn’t sleep. She had imagined that if she had called, they might have said everything they had left unsaid. The book offered something smaller: a conversation about a dog, tomatoes on a counter, an ordinary goodbye.

“I want to borrow it,” she said when Evelyn came to find her.

“You can’t take that one out.”

“Why not?”

“It concerns someone who isn’t here to agree.”

Mara looked up. “My mother is dead.”

“I know. It still concerns her.”

The rule struck Mara as both absurd and cruel. She wanted to ask who had given the library permission to keep the book in the first place. Instead, she closed it and handed it over. Evelyn did not try to soothe her. She put the book back, waited while Mara collected her bag, and held the door open. Outside, the rain had stopped. Mara walked home carrying the dead fern, forgetting entirely about the compost bin.

For three days she looked for the library. On Friday she found a florist between the tailor’s shop and the vacant building. On Saturday there was an alley containing two bins and a bicycle with no wheels. On Sunday she stood across the road for twenty minutes, growing increasingly embarrassed, until the tailor came out to sweep his step and asked whether she needed help. She said she was waiting for someone. He nodded, though there was nowhere sheltered for anyone to wait, and went back inside.

On Monday, rain returned. The florist remained, but a green door had appeared beside it. Mara went in. Evelyn was at the desk, sorting books into piles. The cat was awake and licking a paw.

“I thought I’d imagined this place,” Mara said.

“Many people hope they have.”

“I didn’t.”

Evelyn studied her, then pushed one of the piles aside. “Would you mind helping me? We’ve had more arrivals than usual.”

Mara spent the afternoon recording names on index cards. Some books supplied full names and dates; others gave only a first name, a description, or a place. One belonged to “the woman who waited outside the cinema in a blue coat.” Another concerned “the boy who kept the marble.” Evelyn showed her how to cross-reference them by street, year, and circumstance. The work required patience but little interpretation, which Mara found restful. She did not have to decide whether the almost-events were important. She only had to make sure they could be found.

She returned the next rainy day and the one after that. Evelyn paid her in tea, soup, and occasionally oranges from a grocer who brought them in by the crate. Mara still did her ordinary job, still answered messages, still watered the plants she had not yet killed. But she began watching the weather forecast with an interest that surprised her. On dry evenings she made notes about the catalog, trying to understand its patterns. On wet mornings she brought those notes to the library, where Evelyn would correct them gently and the cat would sit on whatever page was most useful.

One afternoon a boy came in looking for a book about his father. He was perhaps twelve, with a schoolbag held against his chest. His father had moved to another country, he explained, and had not called in several months. The boy wanted to know whether there was a version in which he had stayed. Evelyn asked whether the boy had told his mother where he was going. He had not. She lent him the telephone and waited while he made the call.

There were four books about the boy and his father. Evelyn let him read two: accounts of a fishing trip that had been canceled and a birthday visit postponed by a missed flight. The other two, she said, contained private matters belonging to his father. The boy argued. His face grew red, and he asked why his father’s privacy mattered more than his questions. Evelyn listened without interrupting. Then she said the books might give him answers, but they could not give him his father’s attention, and she was sorry.

The boy left angry, though he thanked Mara for finding his wet gloves. Afterward she asked Evelyn whether the rule had been invented to make the work easier.

“Some days it would be much easier without it,” Evelyn said. “I could hand people whatever they asked for and avoid the argument. But they’d take the stories as proof of things we can’t know.”

“Aren’t they proof?”

“They tell us what almost happened. They don’t tell us what someone owes another person, or what they meant, or what they would do now.”

Mara thought about the boy. She also thought about the green book on the third shelf. She was still angry that she could not borrow it, but she understood the shape of the boundary better than she had before.

Weeks passed. The library grew busy as winter approached. People came in from the rain carrying shopping bags, umbrellas, office folders, and once a covered birdcage. Most left after warming themselves. A few asked questions. A woman read about the job she had nearly accepted in another city and laughed so hard that the cat fled beneath a chair. A man found an account of a bicycle accident that had almost happened when he was nineteen and sat quietly for an hour. Neither seemed eager to know more. They returned their books and went home.

Then, on a morning of thin, persistent rain, Evelyn did not arrive. Mara waited outside for half an hour before the green door appeared. It was unlocked. Inside, the kettle was cold and a new book lay on the desk. It was bound in yellow cloth and had no card tucked inside. Mara opened it and saw Evelyn’s name on the first page.

The account described Evelyn waking with a pain in her chest, deciding it was indigestion, and staying home. It followed her through the morning as she made tea, sat by the window, and considered calling a doctor. At noon she lay down. The story ended there.

Mara read the final note twice. *Evelyn called for help at 8:17 a.m. She was taken to St. Anne’s Hospital.*

Mara checked the clock. It was nearly ten. She found Evelyn’s coat still hanging behind the desk, its pockets containing a handkerchief, a shopping list, and a set of keys. There was no phone number, no address for family. She called the hospital. After several transfers, someone confirmed that Evelyn had been admitted and was receiving care, but could give no further details.

Mara locked the door, put the keys in her pocket, and went to the hospital with the yellow book in her bag.

Evelyn was awake and annoyed by the flowers on her bedside table. A neighbor had sent them, she said, though she had repeatedly told him she disliked lilies. She was pale, but she smiled when Mara appeared.

“You called an ambulance,” Mara said.

“Yes. A sensible decision, which I intend to mention often.”

Mara sat down and took out the book. Evelyn glanced at it, then looked away.

“I know I shouldn’t have read it,” Mara said.

“You were worried.”

“That isn’t permission.”

“No.” Evelyn adjusted the blanket over her knees. “But I’m glad you came.”

For a while they talked about practical things: who would feed the cat, whether the library could remain closed, and how long Evelyn might be in the hospital. Mara offered to look after the place. Evelyn accepted, then asked her to water a plant on the windowsill behind the desk. Mara admitted what had happened to her fern.

“It’s a cactus,” Evelyn said. “You may be qualified.”

At the door, Mara paused. “Do you ever read your own books?”

“I have. Less often than I used to.”

“Does it help?”

“Sometimes. Sometimes it gives me one more thing to think about at three in the morning.”

Mara carried the yellow book back through the rain. At the library she placed it on a high shelf, marked its location on an index card, and left the card in Evelyn’s drawer. Then she fed the cat and opened the curtains. A visitor arrived before she had finished making tea: a woman with a folded umbrella and a question about a sister she had not spoken to in years. Mara listened, found the relevant shelf, and explained the rules as carefully as she could.

That evening, after the visitor left, Mara watered the cactus with a cautious spoonful of water. She checked the locks, turned off the lamps, and stood for a moment by the green book. She did not open it. On her way home she bought tomatoes and bread. At her apartment she ate by the window, then picked up her phone and called an old friend whose messages she had been meaning to answer.

The friend sounded pleased and a little distracted. She was making dinner, and something in the oven needed attention. Mara offered to call back, but her friend told her to stay on the line. They talked while a timer beeped and a cupboard door squeaked. Mara told her about the fern, though not the library. Her friend laughed, described the basil plant she had recently drowned, and invited Mara over the following weekend.

They did not settle anything important. When the call ended, Mara washed her plate and put the remaining tomatoes in a bowl on the counter. Then she wrote down the address her friend had given her, so she would remember where to go.

# The Department of Small Repairs

On the first Tuesday in March, Mara Bell found a brass clock on the steps of the library. It was about the size of a grapefruit, with a glass face and two feet shaped like lion’s paws. Someone had wrapped it in a dish towel and left a note beneath it: **DOES ANYONE HERE KNOW HOW TO FIX THIS?** There was no name, no telephone number, and no explanation of why the owner thought the library might be able to help.

Mara was the library’s facilities manager, which meant she changed lightbulbs, reset the boiler, and called professionals when water appeared in places water should not appear. She knew almost nothing about clocks. Still, she carried it inside rather than leave it in the rain. She set it on the circulation desk beside a jar of pencils and a display of books about early spring gardening.

By noon, six people had asked about it. A retired dentist suggested a shop in the next town, but the shop had closed. A teenager offered to look up a video, but the clock had no visible manufacturer’s name. Mrs. Alvarez, who came in every Tuesday for the large-print mysteries, said her husband used to mend watches, though his hands had become too unsteady for such work. She touched the clock’s glass with one finger and asked if she might bring him to see it.

Mara said yes. This was not an official library service, but neither was keeping spare reading glasses at the desk or letting the chess club store its boards beneath the stairs. The library had accumulated a collection of useful exceptions over the years. Its director, Celia, believed that rules should be clear enough to protect people and flexible enough not to make them miserable. The difficulty, as she often remarked, was knowing which kind of rule you were looking at.

On Wednesday, Mr. Alvarez arrived with his wife and a canvas bag containing a magnifying lens, a tiny screwdriver, and a sandwich. He sat at a table in the local history room, removed the clock’s back, and examined its insides for nearly an hour. Mara passed twice, carrying a ladder. The first time, Mr. Alvarez was silent. The second time, he was eating half his sandwich while explaining the escapement to a boy who had wandered in looking for the bathroom.

By the end of the afternoon, the clock was ticking. It was also gaining four minutes an hour, which Mr. Alvarez considered a respectable start. He asked whether it could remain at the library another day. Celia agreed, provided the clock did not interfere with a school visit scheduled for Thursday. Mara found an empty shelf behind the desk, placed the clock on it, and wrote **PLEASE DO NOT MOVE** on a card. The clock ticked all through the staff’s closing procedures.

Its owner appeared on Friday. She was a woman named June Porter, who taught piano from her home on Ash Street. The clock had belonged to her mother. June had left it at the library because she had seen a notice there for a bicycle repair workshop the previous summer and assumed someone might know somebody. When Mara told her what had happened, June laughed, then apologized for laughing. She had expected to be told off for abandoning it.

Mr. Alvarez came in again that afternoon and showed June the adjustment he had made. The clock now gained only half a minute a day. He told her to watch it for a week and bring it back if necessary. June thanked him, paid nothing because he refused payment, and returned the following morning with a tin of lemon biscuits. The biscuits disappeared before lunchtime. The story of the clock did not disappear nearly so quickly.

The next week, a man brought in a lamp that flickered when its neck was bent. Celia explained that the library did not repair lamps. The man apologized and began wrapping the cord around the base. Before he could leave, another patron looked up from a newspaper and said the switch might be loose. She had worked as an electrician, she explained, though she was retired now. After examining the lamp, she told him where he could buy a replacement switch and offered to show him how to install it.

That evening Celia asked Mara whether she thought the library should hold a repair event. Mara said it would depend on who repaired what, who supervised, and whether anyone planned to plug an unfamiliar appliance into the wall. Celia wrote these concerns on a pad. Underneath them she wrote **ALSO: TABLES, SIGN-UP SHEET, TEA**. By the end of the week, the library had a date, a modest plan, and a notice inviting people to bring broken household objects and practical knowledge.

The event was scheduled for a Saturday in April. Celia found volunteers through the library newsletter, the community college, and a conversation with the owner of the hardware store. The retired electrician, whose name was Ruth Kim, agreed to inspect electrical items but insisted on setting boundaries: nothing connected to the mains would be opened by an amateur, and anything unsafe would be taken away unplugged. A seamstress named Dev offered to mend clothing. Mr. Alvarez said he would look at clocks, provided nobody expected miracles.

Mara prepared the meeting room on Friday evening. She put down protective cloths, arranged the tables, and found an extension lead that had passed its inspection. She made signs for each volunteer and a large one near the entrance that said **REPAIR IS NOT GUARANTEED**. Beneath that, at Celia’s suggestion, she added **ADVICE IS FREE**. Then she went home and tried not to worry that either two hundred people would arrive or nobody would.

Thirty-seven people came, bringing forty-one objects. There were trousers with torn pockets, a wooden chair with a loose leg, a radio that had stopped receiving anything but static, and a porcelain dog whose ear had broken off during a move. Someone brought an umbrella with a bent rib. Someone else brought three umbrellas, hoping to make one good one. A little girl carried a stuffed rabbit with its head tucked under her arm and watched Dev sew it back into place.

Not everything could be saved. Ruth found that the radio needed a component she did not have. The porcelain dog had been glued badly once before, and removing the old adhesive risked taking part of its face with it. The owner decided to keep it as it was. The chair required a clamp larger than any the library possessed. Nevertheless, people stayed. They drank tea, compared notes, and watched work happening at neighboring tables. The man with the chair lent a hand holding a bicycle wheel while someone adjusted its brakes.

At the end of the afternoon, Mara swept thread from the floor and found a single black button beneath a chair. No one claimed it. She put it in a saucer on the windowsill. Celia, looking over the sign-up sheets, said they should do the event again. Mara pointed out that they would need more volunteers and a better system for telling people what could safely be brought in. “Good,” Celia said. “Those sound like solvable problems.”

They held another event in June, then one in September. A volunteer made a simple intake form asking what the object was, what had gone wrong, and whether anyone had attempted a repair already. This last question proved useful. One toaster contained a folded piece of foil placed there by its owner in an attempt to improve the connection. Ruth showed him why that had been dangerous and declined to work on it. He left disappointed but returned the following month with a coat for Dev.

Mara began keeping a ledger, partly to help Celia report on attendance and partly because she liked the details. Beside each item she wrote what had happened to it: **zip replaced**, **needs new cord**, **owner given instructions**, **not repairable here**. She did not record names unless someone wanted to be contacted. By winter, the ledger held more than two hundred entries. Many were ordinary: hems, hinges, plugs, and zippers. A few required longer descriptions, including a snow globe that had leaked onto a photograph sealed inside its base.

The library had other work, of course. Children still came for story hour. Students still arrived before exams and occupied every available table. Mara still dealt with the boiler, which developed a noise like a distant person clearing their throat. The repair events had to fit around all of this. When a volunteer suggested keeping tools permanently in the meeting room, Celia pointed out that the room also hosted tax clinics, language classes, and a support group that needed privacy. They settled on two lockable cupboards in the basement.

In January, the town announced a proposed reduction to the library budget. The building needed roof repairs, and several departments were facing cuts. The proposal would shorten opening hours and leave Mara’s position at twenty hours a week. Celia printed copies and placed them by the entrance. She also encouraged people to attend the council meeting, though she was careful not to suggest that the repair events alone justified the library’s budget. The library was useful in many ways, she said, and people should speak about the ones they knew.

Mara had never addressed the council. She disliked the microphone at the front of the chamber and the timer that counted down each speaker’s three minutes. She prepared notes anyway. At home, she opened the ledger and counted how many items had been brought to the events, how many volunteers had participated, and how many hours the meeting room had been used. The numbers looked small beside the figures in the proposed budget. She nearly put the notes away.

At the meeting, June Porter spoke before her. June described bringing her mother’s clock to the library and meeting Mr. Alvarez. She also spoke about the music books she borrowed and the students she sent there when their families could not afford sheet music. A father described using the computers to complete job applications. A teenager spoke about having somewhere warm to study after school. When Mara’s turn came, she gave the council her figures, then explained what the proposed reduction would mean for routine maintenance. The roof, she noted, would not be the only part of the building to need attention.

The council did not restore the full budget. It approved a smaller reduction, kept the library’s current hours for another year, and allocated money for the most urgent roof work. Mara’s position remained full-time, though an unfilled staff post was eliminated. Celia called the result a partial reprieve. At the next staff meeting, she thanked everyone who had spoken and asked them to help plan for a tighter year. There would be less money for new furniture, fewer printed newsletters, and more grant applications.

That spring, Mara took something of her own to a repair event. It was a small wooden box her father had made when she was a child. He had kept nails in it, sorted by size, until the bottom panel split. After he died, Mara had taken the box home with several of his tools. For three years it had sat on a shelf in her kitchen. She had considered fixing it herself, but each time she picked it up she found some other task to do.

A volunteer named Sam examined the box and said the panel could be replaced, though the wood would not match exactly. Mara hesitated. The old panel had pencil marks on it: measurements, a phone number, and a list of things her father had once needed from the hardware store. Sam suggested attaching a thin piece of wood beneath it instead. The repair would be visible if the box was turned over, but the pencil marks could stay. Mara helped hold the pieces while Sam fitted them together.

When she got home, she put the box back on its shelf. She did not fill it with nails. For a while she left it empty, then began dropping in things she found in her pockets: a key she could not identify, a receipt she needed to keep, a coin from a country she had never visited. Every few months she emptied it and sorted through the contents. The box made that small job easier, and she liked seeing it in use.

In May, the owner of the hardware store donated the large clamp the library had needed at its first repair event. A teenager who had watched Dev mend the stuffed rabbit signed up for a sewing class and later began volunteering at the clothing table. Mr. Alvarez came less often, but he still accepted clocks for examination when he felt well enough. Ruth developed a printed checklist for electrical items, with a space at the bottom where she could write the address of a professional repair shop.

On a rainy Saturday near the end of the school year, Mara opened the meeting room and found a line already forming. A woman held a kitchen drawer against her hip. Behind her stood a boy with a bicycle bell and a man carrying a coat whose lining hung below the hem. Mara set out the intake forms and asked them to write down what they had brought. Then she went to fetch the kettle, checking along the way that the roof above the stairs was still dry.

# The Shop for Unfinished Things

The clock in Mara’s window had been seven minutes slow for eleven years. People sometimes stopped to tell her, pointing through the glass with the satisfaction of someone who had noticed a loose button on a stranger’s coat. Mara thanked them and explained that the clock was not for sale. Its hands moved, its pendulum swung, and every Sunday it lost precisely seven minutes. Her husband had repaired it the week before he died, and she had never found the heart to correct his work.

The shop occupied a narrow brick building between a bakery and a vacant lot. Its sign read **REPAIRS**, though Mara repaired fewer things than she used to. Manufacturers had grown fond of sealed cases, special screws, and components that cost almost as much as the machines they inhabited. Still, people brought her lamps, radios, fans, and the occasional object they could not name. She kept a box under the counter for mysteries: pieces of metal and plastic whose owners had said, “It fell off, but everything seems to be working.”

On a wet Tuesday in March, a girl came in carrying a toaster wrapped in a blue towel. She was perhaps sixteen, with rain darkening the shoulders of her school uniform. She placed the bundle on the counter and explained that the toaster belonged to her grandmother. It had stopped working that morning, and her grandmother was convinced the house would burn down if anyone plugged it in again. The girl did not share this concern, but she did want toast.

Mara turned the toaster over. A crumb tray slid out, depositing a small brown dune on the counter. The girl watched closely as Mara removed the screws and lifted the casing.

“Do you know what you’re looking for?” she asked.

“Not yet,” Mara said. “First I’m looking at what’s there.”

A strip of bread had become wedged near the latch, keeping it from catching. Mara removed it with tweezers, brushed out the crumbs, and tested the mechanism. The toaster clicked down and stayed. She plugged it in briefly, watching the elements glow.

“How much?” the girl asked.

“Nothing this time. It took three minutes.”

The girl frowned. “You knew which three minutes.”

Her name was Leila, and she returned on Saturday with a desk lamp from her bedroom. The switch worked if held at a particular angle, which made reading difficult and occasionally alarming. Mara showed her how to unplug the lamp, open the base, and examine the connections. A wire had worked loose from its terminal. Leila tightened it herself, then put the lamp back together without being asked. When she finished, she stayed to help sort the screws that had accumulated in a biscuit tin.

By April, Leila came most weekends. She swept the floor, labelled drawers, and learned to tell Mara when she had no idea what she was doing. This was harder than learning the names of tools. Leila was quick and hated pausing in the middle of a task, especially when a customer was watching. Mara made her stop anyway. An hour spent reading a diagram, she said, could save a day spent explaining why someone’s grandfather’s radio was now two radios, neither of them functional.

Leila brought questions from school, too. She wanted to know why some materials conducted electricity and others didn’t, why rechargeable batteries eventually failed, and why Mara marked certain repairs in a red notebook. The notebook, Mara explained, was for jobs she had declined or mishandled. She recorded what had happened and what she might do differently. Leila flipped through it one afternoon and found pages of careful notes, including several labelled **COULD NOT FIX**.

“You kept all these?” she asked.

“They’re useful,” Mara said. “Besides, I remember them whether I write them down or not.”

At the end of April, a notice appeared on the shop door. The town council was considering a flood-control plan for the riverfront, including the block where the shop stood. Engineers had found that the existing embankment would not protect the lowest streets during a severe flood. One proposal called for a wider channel, a raised path, and the removal of fourteen buildings. The notice invited residents and business owners to a meeting at the library. It used the phrase *managed retreat*, which Mara read twice before folding the paper and putting it beneath the cash register.

The river had flooded before, though not badly in Mara’s lifetime. Every few years it climbed over the lower bank and filled the car park behind the grocery store. Children came to look at the water; adults moved their cars and compared the depth with previous years. Older residents talked about a flood decades earlier that had reached the railway tracks. There were photographs of it in the local history room, but the river had since been straightened and the banks reinforced. Most people treated those photographs as history.

Mara’s lease would expire in eighteen months. If the council approved the plan, the building’s owner could sell to the town, and the shop would have to move. Mara told herself she ought to be relieved. Her knees hurt when she stood for too long, the roof leaked near the back shelves, and she had been trying for three years to reduce her hours. Yet when she pictured the shop empty, she kept seeing the outlines left by everything she would remove: pale rectangles on the wall, screw holes, dustless patches beneath the cabinets.

Leila attended the meeting with her grandmother. Mara sat behind them, near the aisle. An engineer named Owen presented maps showing projected water levels under several scenarios. He spoke carefully about uncertainty: rainfall could vary, the timing of storms mattered, and no plan would eliminate every risk. The wider channel, he said, would give the river room to rise without forcing as much water into the streets. A woman from the council described compensation for property owners and a proposed relocation fund for businesses, though the amount available had not yet been settled.

During questions, a man from the bakery asked why the town could not simply build a higher wall. Owen said a wall was one option, but it would need to extend well beyond the affected block. It would also require pumps for rainwater trapped on the town side. The costs and maintenance would be substantial. Someone else asked whether the new channel would protect the houses downstream. Owen said the modelling suggested it would not worsen flooding there, but the town was commissioning a further review.

People left the meeting with different pieces of the presentation in mind. Some repeated the largest estimate of possible damage; others repeated the lowest. The bakery owner began a petition against demolition. A family living near the river put their house up for sale. At the hardware store, two men argued over whether the council had neglected the embankment or whether the plans were an excuse to redevelop the waterfront. Mara signed neither petition nor letter. She wanted to understand the decision, though she was beginning to suspect that understanding it would not make her like it.

In May, Leila brought an old portable radio into the shop. Its brown case was scuffed at the corners, and the handle had been replaced with a strip of leather. It had belonged to her grandfather, who had died when she was small. Her grandmother wanted to know whether it could receive the evening news again. Leila placed it on the bench with unusual care. She had few memories of her grandfather, but she remembered the radio on his kitchen table and the sound of him turning its dial.

The battery compartment was corroded. Mara showed Leila how to clean the contacts safely, and together they checked the wiring. A capacitor needed replacing, and the tuning cord had slipped from its track. They ordered the component and spent the following Saturday threading the cord around tiny wheels. Leila grew frustrated when it slipped for the fourth time. Mara suggested a break. They ate pastries on the back step, then returned to the bench and found that a spring had been hooked into the wrong hole.

When the radio finally worked, it produced a burst of static, followed by a man discussing the price of wheat. Leila laughed so loudly that a customer at the counter looked over. They turned the dial through music, traffic reports, and a station broadcasting in a language neither of them knew. The sound was thin and uneven, but it filled the room. Leila took a photograph for her grandmother, then stayed another hour to polish the case with a soft cloth.

The next week, her grandmother came by to thank Mara and brought an envelope of photographs. One showed the street outside the shop during the old flood. Water covered the pavement and reached halfway up a delivery van’s wheels. Another showed Leila’s grandfather standing on a ladder, passing boxes through an upstairs window. On the back he had written the date and the words **MOVED THE RECORDS JUST IN TIME**. Mara borrowed the photographs for the afternoon and walked them over to the library, where the history room kept a file on the flood.

The librarian found newspaper reports and a handwritten log kept by the fire station. The reports described evacuations, damaged roads, and volunteers carrying food to residents who could not leave their homes. The log listed calls with times and addresses, including several from the street where Mara’s shop now stood. It was useful evidence of what had happened, though it could not settle what might happen next. The riverbank was different now, as were the buildings and drainage systems. Mara made copies anyway, with the librarian’s permission, and brought them to Leila.

They spread the copies across the workbench after closing. Leila noticed that the fire station had recorded water entering the basement of the old printworks before anyone reported flooding on the road. The printworks had stood where the vacant lot was now. Mara found a note about a blocked drain two streets uphill. They began marking the addresses on a modern map, using different colours for road closures, flooded buildings, and rescue calls. By the time they stopped, the bakery next door had turned off its lights.

At the next council meeting, Mara brought the map. She did not offer it as proof that the proposed channel was necessary. Instead, she asked whether the engineers had used the fire station records and whether the blocked drains had been accounted for in the new modelling. Owen said he had seen some of the newspaper reports but not the complete log. He asked the librarian for copies and promised to pass the drainage question to the review team. Mara was glad she had spoken, even though her voice had shaken.

The council held two more meetings over the summer. The independent review supported the main findings but recommended changes to the downstream drainage plan. The proposed business relocation fund was increased after several owners described the cost of moving equipment and losing customers during a closure. The bakery owner still opposed demolition. So did Mara’s landlord, who submitted an alternative wall design for consideration. The engineers reviewed it and published a comparison. It would protect the block, they concluded, but would cost more over its expected life and leave less room for future changes to the river.

In August, the council voted to proceed with the channel. The work would be phased over several years, beginning downstream. Property purchases would take time, and the fourteen buildings would not all come down at once. There was applause from a few people in the chamber and angry shouting from others. Mara went home carrying a thick packet of documents. She put it on her kitchen table and left it there for a week, moving it aside each evening to make room for her plate.

Leila expected Mara to announce her retirement. Instead, one Saturday morning, Mara asked her to help measure the shop. They wrote down the dimensions of the benches, shelving, cabinets, and largest pieces of equipment. The measurements filled several sheets. Mara had seen a small unit for rent near the bus station, farther from the river. Its front window was plain, and the floor sloped slightly, but it had enough power outlets and a dry storeroom. She had not yet decided whether to take it.

They visited the unit together. Leila stood in the empty room, imagining the counter against one wall and the workbenches beneath the window. Mara checked the taps and looked closely at the ceiling. Outside, buses arrived and departed, bringing people from neighbourhoods that rarely passed the old shop. The rent was higher, but the relocation fund would cover some of the moving costs. After a week of calculations and an uncomfortable conversation with her accountant, Mara signed a lease beginning in January.

Word spread that the shop was moving. Customers came in to collect objects they had forgotten, including a hair dryer repaired eight months earlier and a brass lamp whose owner had moved away. Others brought new work, hoping to have it finished before the move. Mara began turning away large jobs she could not complete in time. Leila made a list of everything that needed packing and discovered, behind a cabinet, the missing back of a television that had left the shop years ago. They added it to the box of mysteries.

On the final afternoon, neighbours came to help carry the heavy benches into a rented van. The baker brought a tray of rolls; Leila’s grandmother wrapped the clock in old curtains. Mara walked through the rooms after everyone had gone outside. The shelves were bare, and the marks on the walls were just as she had imagined. She checked the cupboards, turned off the lights, and locked the door. Then she went back in because she had forgotten the red notebook on the windowsill.

The new shop opened three weeks later. On its first Saturday, a man arrived with a fan that rattled, followed by a woman carrying a kettle with a damaged handle. Leila took their names and wrote careful descriptions of the problems. Mara unwrapped the old clock and set it in the window, where it began its slow weekly drift. At closing time, Leila asked whether they should put up a notice explaining that it lost seven minutes.

“Let’s see how many people tell us first,” Mara said.

They locked the door and caught the bus home, leaving the clock swinging in the window.

# The Department of Lost Sounds

On the morning the church bell disappeared, nobody noticed at first.

The bell had rung at seven every day for a hundred and eleven years. It marked the opening of the bakery, the unlocking of the school gates, and the moment when Mr. Vale, who had retired from the railway in 1986, rose from his chair and announced that he supposed he ought to do something with himself.

That Tuesday, the bell did not ring.

The baker opened late. Three children arrived at school in their pajamas, having slept through their mothers’ calls. Mr. Vale remained in his chair until nearly nine, staring at the window and feeling, without knowing why, that the day had begun improperly.

The bell was still in the tower. The rope still hung beside the stairs. When the vicar pulled it, the great bronze mouth moved back and forth exactly as it should.

No sound came out.

At noon, the vicar telephoned the Department of Lost Sounds.

Mara Bellamy answered on the third ring. She had worked for the department for nineteen years and knew better than to say, “How can I help you?” People who called had usually tried everyone else, and most were embarrassed.

“Department of Lost Sounds,” she said. “What have you lost?”

“A bell,” said the vicar.

“The whole bell?”

“No. Just the sound.”

Mara opened a fresh file.

The department occupied the basement of a municipal building that had once been a public swimming pool. The pool was covered over now, but the tiles remained, pale blue squares beneath the filing cabinets. In damp weather, the room smelled faintly of chlorine and old paper.

There were four employees: Mara; her supervisor, Mr. Chao; a technician named Dev, who repaired the listening equipment; and an intern named Alice, who had applied by mistake and stayed because she liked the work.

They recovered all sorts of sounds. Some were valuable, like the last recording of a singer whose voice had been destroyed in a fire. Some were ordinary: a grandfather’s whistle, a dog’s particular bark, the creak of a stair in a demolished house. Once, they had spent eleven weeks tracking down the noise made by a certain kind of orange wrapping machine, because a woman remembered falling asleep to it while her mother worked the night shift.

Their methods were difficult to explain, partly because Mr. Chao discouraged explanations and partly because the equipment had been assembled from things that should not have worked together. There were microphones, certainly, but also copper wire, tuning forks, a gramophone horn, and a glass jar containing a small amount of seawater.

The jar had belonged to Mr. Chao’s predecessor. Nobody knew what the water did. When Alice asked whether they could remove it and see what happened, Mr. Chao said that was precisely the sort of question that had led to the closing of the old acoustics laboratory.

By two o’clock, Mara and Alice were on the train to the town.

“You’ve never had a church bell before?” Alice asked.

“Not a whole one.”

“What’s the largest sound you’ve recovered?”

“A thunderstorm.”

Alice looked up from her notebook.

“Only part of it,” Mara said. “It had gone missing from a film. The editor remembered the storm being louder when they shot it. He thought someone had altered the recording, but no one had. We found the thunder in a warehouse, caught between two sheets of packing foam.”

“How did it get there?”

“We didn’t ask.”

Alice made a note anyway.

The town was small enough that the station had no ticket barriers and large enough that people argued about whether it was becoming a city. The vicar met them in a green coat and led them uphill past the bakery, where a handwritten sign said SORRY FOR THE LATE START.

Inside the church tower, Mara examined the bell. It was engraved with a date, the names of three donors, and a line from a poem about waking the valley. Its bronze surface bore the soft discolorations of age.

She put her hand against it while the vicar pulled the rope. She felt the vibration travel through her palm and into her wrist. Alice held a microphone beneath the bell, listening through headphones.

“Nothing,” Alice said.

“Any repairs recently?” Mara asked.

“Not to the bell.”

“Has anyone made a recording of it?”

“Of course. Several, I should think. There’s one on the parish website.”

“Does it still sound?”

The vicar hesitated. “I haven’t checked.”

They went downstairs and gathered around his laptop. The parish website had photographs of the church fête, notices about roof repairs, and a video titled *Sunday Bells*. In the video, the tower stood against a blue sky while birds crossed the frame.

The bell moved.

There was no sound.

Alice checked the volume, then played a different video. An advertisement for garden furniture came through the speakers at startling volume.

The vicar closed the laptop.

“That’s rather worse than I expected.”

Mara took a small receiver from her bag and switched it on. A red needle moved across a numbered dial. She walked slowly through the church, stopping at each doorway. Near the font, the needle twitched. Beside the organ, it held steady. At the back door, it swung sharply to the right.

“Something went out this way,” she said.

“Can you tell when?” asked Alice.

“Recently.”

The back door opened onto a narrow lane. Mara followed the needle past bins, a stack of roof tiles, and a wall covered with ivy. At the end of the lane, it settled back to zero.

The bell’s sound had reached the street. After that, it could have gone anywhere.

They spent the afternoon interviewing people. The baker had heard nothing unusual. The school caretaker had noticed that the birds seemed louder than usual, though he admitted he might simply have been listening more carefully. A woman walking a terrier said she had seen a man standing outside the church before dawn, but she described him as “tallish, with a face,” which gave Alice little to write down.

At four, Mara bought tea from a café and spread her notes across a table. Alice drew a map of the streets around the church.

“Could someone have taken it?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“Why would they?”

“Sometimes people take things because they don’t know how to ask for them.”

“That sounds very wise.”

“It was in our training manual.”

Alice looked up. Mara smiled.

The training manual was forty years old and mostly concerned with electrical safety. Its only advice on dealing with the public was never to tell a caller that a lost sound had “probably gone for good.” Mr. Chao had underlined the sentence twice.

At the next table, an older man folded his newspaper.

“You’re the people from the council,” he said.

“Not exactly,” said Mara.

“I heard you talking to Mrs. Foster about the bell.”

The man introduced himself as Mr. Vale. He lived across from the church and had heard the bell every morning since his marriage, except for the years he had worked the early shift at the railway.

“My wife used to complain about it,” he said. “Said there was no need to announce seven o’clock to the entire county. But when they stopped it for repairs one summer, she kept waking me to ask the time.”

“When was that?” Mara asked.

“Nineteen ninety-four, perhaps. They had scaffolding up for weeks.”

“Did you hear it yesterday morning?”

“Yes. Same as always.”

“Anything different afterward?”

Mr. Vale thought for a while. “There was a young fellow outside the church. Sat on the wall with his head in his hands. I asked if he was all right, but he didn’t answer.”

“Did you recognize him?”

“No. He had a blue coat, though. Railway blue.”

Alice looked at Mara. The woman with the terrier had mentioned a blue coat too; they had left it out because she had been uncertain whether it was blue or gray.

“Which way did he go?” Mara asked.

“Toward the station. I saw him from my window.”

The stationmaster knew the young man. His name was Lewis, and he had been sleeping in the old waiting room for the past three nights.

“I told him he couldn’t stay,” she said. “But the last train gets in late, and it’s cold. I leave the side door unlocked sometimes.”

“Is he there now?”

“He went out this morning. Left his bag.”

The waiting room had a bench, a radiator that worked unevenly, and a poster advertising a seaside resort whose pier had burned down fifteen years earlier. A canvas bag sat beneath the bench. On top of it lay a blue railway coat, neatly folded.

Mara’s receiver began to hum.

Alice crouched beside the bag. “Should we open it?”

“Not without him.”

The stationmaster made a telephone call. Half an hour later, Lewis arrived carrying a paper cup of soup and a loaf of bread. He stopped in the doorway when he saw them.

The stationmaster explained who they were. Lewis set the soup down very carefully.

“I didn’t steal anything,” he said.

“We haven’t said you did,” Mara replied.

He looked at the bag.

“Can I see what’s inside?” she asked.

He opened it himself. There were clothes, a toothbrush, two paperback books, and a small wooden box. The box had a brass clasp and a crack across the lid.

The receiver’s needle pressed against the end of the dial.

“Where did you get that?” Mara asked.

“It was my mum’s.”

“May I?”

Lewis handed it to her. The box was light. When she opened the clasp, she heard nothing, but the hairs on her arms rose. She closed it again.

“What’s in it?” Alice asked.

“I don’t know,” Lewis said. “It was on her dressing table. She kept earrings in it.”

“Did you take it to the church?”

He nodded.

His mother had died six weeks earlier. He had been clearing her house, working through cupboards and drawers while his older sister handled the paperwork. They had grown up in the town, but he had moved away after school. The house was being sold, and he had come back to collect the last of his things.

“I thought I’d finished,” he said. “Then I found her coat behind the kitchen door. I couldn’t leave it there, but I couldn’t put it in a bag either.”

He had walked out before dawn, carrying the box because it had been in his hand when he left. He sat outside the church until the bell rang.

“When we were kids, she’d open our curtains when it rang,” he said. “Every morning. Even on Saturdays, which we hated.” He rubbed his thumb against the edge of the box. “I sat there thinking I’d forgotten how it sounded. I’d forgotten her voice too. I kept trying to hear either one.”

He had opened the box without thinking. Afterward, he could not remember closing it.

Mara asked if she could take it outside. Lewis followed them onto the platform, where the stationmaster had gone back to her office. A train was due in twelve minutes.

Mara placed the box on the bench and opened the lid.

At first there was only the ordinary noise of the station: a distant engine, wind in the wires, a pigeon moving under the roof. Then a single note emerged, so low that Alice felt it in her ribs before she heard it. The note widened, gathering overtones, until the platform seemed to tremble around them.

The church bell rang once.

Lewis flinched. The sound continued, rolling down the tracks and over the rooftops. People emerged from the station office and the shop across the road. Somewhere uphill, a dog began to bark.

The bell rang a second time, then a third. It gave seven slow strikes before the sound faded.

Alice looked at her watch. It was nearly six.

From the church tower, faint but unmistakable, came another ring. The vicar was trying the rope.

Lewis sat down on the bench. He kept the empty box in his lap.

“I didn’t mean to take it,” he said.

“I know,” said Mara.

“Will it stay there now?”

“I think so. The vicar will call if it doesn’t.”

He ran his fingers over the crack in the lid. “I was hoping I’d hear her when you opened it.”

Mara sat beside him. She had brought a recorder from the department, and for a moment she considered offering to search. But Lewis had not reported a missing voice. His mother’s voice might still be on a telephone message, or a video, or an answering machine in a cupboard. It might return to him unexpectedly while he was washing a plate. The department could not promise any of those things.

“Do you have recordings of her?” she asked.

“My sister does. I haven’t wanted to listen yet.”

The approaching train sounded its horn beyond the bend. Alice moved the equipment off the bench to make room for the passengers gathering on the platform.

“You can keep the box,” Mara said.

Lewis gave a short laugh. “I was going to ask.”

He stayed on the bench after the train arrived. As Mara and Alice boarded, he stood and thanked them. Then he went back into the waiting room to fetch his soup.

On the journey home, Alice wrote up their notes. The bell’s recovery required only a page. She spent longer on Lewis’s account, crossing out several sentences before she was satisfied.

“Do you think the box really took it?” she asked.

“The receiver says it did.”

“I mean, do you think he did it somehow?”

“I don’t know.”

Alice looked out at the fields passing in the dusk. “He wanted to hear something, and then he couldn’t bear to let it go.”

“Perhaps.”

“You don’t have a theory?”

“I have several,” Mara said. “I’ve learned to be careful about putting them in the file.”

Back at the department, Mr. Chao listened to their report and signed the forms. Dev checked the receiver and found a thin coating of bronze-colored dust inside its casing. He collected it in an envelope, labeled it, and put it in a drawer with other substances that had appeared in the equipment over the years.

The next morning, the vicar telephoned.

“The bell rang at seven,” he said. “And I’ve checked the video. It’s back there too.”

“Good,” said Mara.

“There is one small thing. It seems a little louder than before.”

From his tone, she thought he might be pleased about this.

“Give it a few days,” she said. “It may settle.”

That afternoon, a woman called about the sound of rain on her childhood bedroom window. The house had been demolished, and she had found that rain on her current windows did not sound the same. She apologized twice for bothering them.

Mara opened a fresh file and asked what she remembered about the room.

“There was an apple tree outside,” the woman said. “The branches tapped the glass when it was windy. I’d forgotten that until just now.”

Mara wrote it down. They might be able to help; an apple tree changed the sound of rain, and its branches gave them something particular to look for. She asked the woman for the address of the old house and whether she had any photographs.

Across the room, Alice was testing microphones. Dev had taken the seawater jar from the shelf and was wiping dust from beneath it, working carefully so that the water did not spill. The telephone rang again before Mara had finished the call.

It was an ordinary busy afternoon. Somewhere, a sound had gone missing, and someone had begun to describe it.

# The Things We Learn to Mend

The first object I ever saw repaired was a toaster, although “repaired” may give the event more dignity than it deserves. My father unplugged it, turned it upside down over a newspaper, and shook it until a small avalanche of crumbs fell out. Then he plugged it in again, pressed the lever, and waited. When the toast emerged, he gave a short nod, as if the appliance had apologized.

For years I believed that was what repair meant: removing the obvious obstruction and allowing a thing to resume its duties. Later I learned about loose connections, worn bearings, cracked solder, swollen capacitors, and the astonishing range of failures hidden inside ordinary objects. I also learned that a great many things cannot be fixed by shaking them over a newspaper, though it remains an appealing first step.

The repair café opened on a Saturday in March, in a room behind the public library. Someone had hung a paper sign on the door. The letters were uneven and the word “café” was missing its accent, but there was coffee inside, and there were people willing to look at broken things. That seemed sufficient.

I went because I had a lamp that flickered. I had already replaced the bulb twice and tried it in three outlets. Each time, the light came on brightly, dimmed, brightened again, and then settled into a faint, nervous pulse. I had begun to suspect that the lamp was haunted, but I thought it polite to consult an electrician before a priest.

The room smelled of coffee and machine oil. Four folding tables had been arranged in a square, each covered with tools. A woman in a green cardigan was examining a radio. A man with magnifying glasses balanced on his forehead was sewing a torn backpack. At the far table, an older volunteer was trying to explain to a young boy why the wheel had come off his toy truck.

“Too much weight?” the boy asked.

“Possibly,” said the volunteer.

“It was carrying dinosaurs.”

“Well,” the volunteer said, “that would do it.”

A woman at the sign-in desk took my name and wrote “lamp, flickers” on a paper ticket. She asked me to wait. I sat beside a man holding a food processor in both arms, as though it were a baby he did not quite trust.

After a few minutes, the woman with the radio called me over. Her name was Lena. She was a retired electrical engineer, and she looked at the lamp with the calm attention of someone who had spent a long time learning not to be impressed by plastic.

She checked that it was unplugged. Then she unscrewed the base, exposing the wire connections.

“Did you buy this new?” she asked.

“About eight years ago.”

“Do you remember where?”

I did. It had come from a shop that sold inexpensive furniture in flat boxes. I had bought it during the first week in an apartment where I knew nobody, when I had decided that a lamp, a plant, and a set of matching bowls would make me into a person who lived somewhere on purpose. The plant had died. Two of the bowls had chipped. The lamp had lasted.

Lena touched a connection with the tip of a screwdriver.

“This is loose,” she said. “See?”

I leaned closer. I could see a small metal terminal and a wire attached to it, but I could not honestly see what made it loose. Lena put the screwdriver in my hand and showed me how to test it. The screw turned more easily than I expected.

“That would explain the flickering,” she said.

She tightened the connection, inspected the rest of the wiring, and reassembled the base. Then she plugged in the lamp. It shone steadily.

The whole operation took perhaps seven minutes. I thanked her, and she waved me toward the coffee, where someone had set out a plate of biscuits. I stayed for an hour.

At the next table, the man with the food processor learned that its motor was probably fine but its safety latch had snapped. A volunteer found a replacement part online and wrote down the model number for him. The boy’s truck received a small screw through its axle. The backpack got a row of stitches that looked sturdier than the original seam. The radio, unfortunately, went home silent; its owner was given the address of a specialist shop and advised to ask for an estimate before committing to anything.

Nobody applauded. There were no dramatic transformations. Mostly, people bent over objects, asked questions, and passed tools to one another. But the room had an atmosphere I recognized without immediately being able to name it. It felt like a place where difficulty was permitted.

In many parts of life, the broken thing must be removed quickly from view. The printer jams just before a meeting, the zipper catches when you are late, the chair begins to wobble while someone is visiting. We experience the failure as an interruption, and often as a small accusation: you should have bought something better, maintained it properly, noticed the warning signs. At the repair café, a broken object was not an embarrassment. It was the reason everyone was there.

I returned the following month with nothing to fix. The woman at the desk remembered the lamp and asked whether it was still working. When I said yes, she handed me a stack of tickets and suggested I could help with sign-in.

That was how I became a volunteer, though for a while my contribution was mostly making coffee and writing descriptions of mysterious problems. People brought in kettles that refused to boil, headphones that only worked on one side, coats with damaged zippers, a cuckoo clock that had stopped speaking, and a pair of garden shears so rusted they looked as if they had been recovered from a shipwreck.

My favorite ticket read: “Fan makes a noise like a frightened horse.” The volunteer who took the job considered this description carefully, turned on the fan, and said, “Yes, I hear it.”

Not every object had an interesting story, and not every story had a happy ending. A ceramic bowl arrived in a bag of fragments after falling from a kitchen shelf. Its owner had made it in an evening class twenty years earlier. A volunteer spread the pieces on a towel and found that several small shards were missing. They could glue the larger pieces together, she explained, but the bowl would not hold soup again.

The owner considered this. Then she said she had never liked eating soup from it anyway. She had always been worried about dropping it.

When she came back at the end of the afternoon, the bowl was whole enough to sit on a shelf. Pale lines ran between the pieces. She held it in both hands and turned it toward the window.

“It looks older,” she said.

“It is older,” the volunteer replied.

At home, I began to notice the quiet negotiations taking place between people and their possessions. A neighbor tied the handle of a kitchen drawer with string because the screw kept falling out. A friend learned to patch jeans from videos and became so practiced that she started adding bright fabric under the holes. My mother kept a rubber band around the battery cover of her television remote for almost a decade, replacing the band whenever it snapped. None of these solutions would have appeared in a product catalog. They worked because someone had looked at a particular problem and decided that it was worth a few minutes of thought.

There is a pleasure in that attention. Modern objects often arrive with their workings hidden. Their cases are sealed, their screws are unusual, their parts are too small or too specialized for a person without training to replace. Sometimes that design makes sense: a device may need to be waterproof, or safe from casual tampering, or small enough to fit in a pocket. But it can also make the user feel like a guest in their own home, surrounded by possessions whose inner lives are none of their business.

Repair changes the relationship. Even when the attempt fails, opening a thing reveals that it was made. The seamless surface gives way to clips, wires, fasteners, labels, and decisions. Someone chose where the cable would run. Someone decided how thick a bracket needed to be. Someone designed a part that could be replaced, or one that would require replacing half the machine.

This knowledge does not turn everyone into an engineer. It does, however, make the world slightly less magical and slightly more interesting.

One afternoon a woman named Priya brought in a sewing machine that had belonged to her grandmother. She carried it in a hard case with a yellowed handle. The machine was heavy, dark blue, and decorated with a silver line that curved along its side. Priya said it had stopped feeding fabric forward. She could hear the motor running, but the stitches gathered in one place.

The sewing volunteer, Marisol, asked when it had last been used.

“My grandmother used it every week,” Priya said. “She died three years ago. I haven’t touched it much since.”

Marisol set the machine on the table and removed the needle plate. Lint had collected underneath in a dense gray mat. She fetched a brush and worked patiently around the feed dogs, the little metal teeth that move fabric under the needle. Priya watched, then asked if she could try.

For the next half hour, they cleaned and tested the machine together. Marisol showed Priya where to place a drop of oil and how to turn the handwheel to see the mechanism move. Priya found an old pin caught beneath the bobbin case. When she lifted it out with tweezers, she laughed.

“My grandmother used to keep pins in her mouth,” she said. “Everyone told her not to. She said if she swallowed one, she’d simply sew her insides back together.”

Eventually they threaded the machine and placed a scrap of cotton beneath the presser foot. Priya pressed the pedal. The needle rose and fell, and the fabric traveled steadily through.

She stopped after a few inches. The seam was crooked, but it held.

Marisol suggested practicing on scraps before attempting a garment. Priya nodded, folded the little piece of cotton, and put it in her pocket.

I thought about that scrap afterward. It was not valuable fabric, and the stitching was not especially neat. But it gave Priya evidence that the machine could still do what she remembered, and perhaps that she could learn to use it without her grandmother standing beside her. The repair had addressed a mechanical problem, but it had also opened a possibility that had been closed for three years.

It is tempting to say that everything can be mended if only we have enough patience. The repair café taught me the opposite. Some things cannot be restored. Parts break in ways that make an object unsafe. Materials deteriorate beyond recovery. A replacement component costs more than anyone can reasonably spend. Sometimes the owner has already tried several fixes, and another attempt would only consume an afternoon that could be used elsewhere.

Learning to repair includes learning when to stop.

Lena was especially good at these conversations. She never declared an object hopeless from across the room. She would examine it, explain what she found, and distinguish between “I can’t fix this today,” “this needs a specialist,” and “I don’t think this should be used again.” Those are different judgments, though people often hear them as the same.

Once, a man brought in an electric blanket with a damaged cord. Lena inspected it and shook her head.

“Couldn’t you just tape it?” he asked.

“No,” she said. Then, seeing his disappointment, she added, “Not safely.”

He told her the blanket had been a gift from his sister. He used it every winter. Lena listened, but she did not soften the answer. They talked instead about replacing it and about saving the fabric cover, which his sister had sewn herself.

He left with the blanket still broken. He also left knowing why.

That distinction matters. A repair volunteer does not have to produce a working object to offer something useful. Sometimes the useful thing is an explanation. Sometimes it is a warning. Sometimes it is permission to stop trying without feeling foolish.

Outside the café, the word “repair” is often used for less tangible matters: friendships, neighborhoods, institutions, the damage done by careless words. These comparisons can be helpful, but only up to a point. People are not lamps. We do not come with wiring diagrams, and a relationship cannot be unplugged while someone safely investigates the fault.

Still, a few habits from the workbench seem worth carrying elsewhere. Look closely before deciding what is wrong. Ask what has already been tried. Do not force a part simply because you are impatient. Be honest about what you know and what you do not. If you make a promise about the result, make it a modest one.

And listen to the person who lives with the problem. At the café, the owner often knew something no volunteer could see: the kettle only failed after the water had already warmed; the zipper caught near the same tooth every time; the radio worked if it was tilted toward the window. These details might sound incidental until they lead someone to the fault.

The repair café eventually moved into a larger room. We acquired better lighting, more chairs, and a proper cabinet for tools. A local hardware shop donated screws and washers. Someone brought in a label maker, which led to a brief period of excessive organization: drawers were labeled, shelves were labeled, and the label maker itself received a label reading “LABEL MAKER.”

I learned to replace a plug under supervision. I learned to sew on buttons well enough that they stayed attached. I learned how much dust a desktop fan can collect, and that several people will gather around almost anything if you say, “That’s strange,” in the right tone.

The lamp on my desk still works. I sometimes think of replacing it because its shade has faded and the switch feels a little stiff. Then I turn it on, and the light falls across the desk exactly as it always has. I find that I have no pressing reason to change it.

Last autumn, near closing time, a girl came in carrying a stuffed fox. One of its ears had torn loose, and a narrow strip of stuffing protruded from the seam. She held the fox by its middle and explained that the ear had caught on a fence when she was climbing down.

Marisol offered to sew it back on. The girl agreed, but only after establishing that the fox would remain in the room and that she could watch.

Marisol chose orange thread from a box and threaded a needle. The girl sat beside her, holding the fox steady while the stitches went in. She asked whether the needle hurt him. Marisol said she thought he was being very brave. The girl considered this answer and accepted it.

When the ear was attached, Marisol handed the fox back. The girl inspected the seam, ran a finger along it, and tilted the fox’s head from side to side.

“It’s a little crooked,” she said.

“It is,” Marisol agreed. “I can try again if you want.”

The girl looked at the fox for another moment. Then she tucked him under her arm.

“No,” she said. “He looks like he’s listening.”

They left together. Marisol put away her needle, and I folded the empty chairs. On the table lay a few short lengths of orange thread, too small to use. I gathered them into my palm and dropped them in the bin. Then we turned off the lights and locked the library door.
