samples.result:
# The Things a Library Keeps

At eight in the morning, before the library opens, the building belongs to its sounds. The heating pipes knock behind the walls. A cart rolls over the seam between carpet and tile, giving a small double bump each time. Somewhere near the back, a printer wakes with the mechanical determination of a creature preparing to defend its territory. Outside, buses sigh at the curb. Inside, the lights come on one row at a time, revealing tables with their chairs tucked in, shelves that look orderly from a distance, and a blue mitten someone left beneath the newspaper rack yesterday.

Mara, who has worked at the library for eleven years, puts the mitten on the lost-and-found shelf. It joins a travel mug, two pairs of reading glasses, a single earring shaped like a silver leaf, and an umbrella so small it seems designed for a very optimistic person. Most of these things will never be claimed. The glasses might be; people notice their absence quickly. But the mitten has already spent a cold night away from its owner, and Mara suspects that by afternoon it will have been replaced.

There are tasks to do before anyone arrives. The returned books must be checked in and sorted. The public computers need to be turned on. Someone has to refill the paper in the printer, straighten the chairs in the children’s room, and make sure the bathroom has soap. None of these jobs appears in the bronze plaque by the entrance, which describes the library as a place dedicated to knowledge, imagination, and the free exchange of ideas. They are nevertheless part of making those things available. It is hard to exchange ideas freely when the printer has run out of paper and you need a form before noon.

At nine, Mara unlocks the doors. The first person in is usually Mr. Bell, who reads three newspapers and leaves before lunch. He says good morning in a voice that sounds as though it has traveled a long way to reach him. On Mondays he complains about the football scores; on Thursdays he complains about the city council. He has opinions on nearly everything, but he expresses them gently, as if he is offering each one for inspection rather than asking anyone to accept it.

Today, though, the first visitor is a woman carrying a cardboard box. She sets it on the desk with both arms wrapped around it.

“These were my mother’s,” she says.

Inside are travel guides, gardening manuals, and a collection of mysteries with cracked spines. Mara explains that the library cannot add every donated book to its collection. Some may go to the book sale; others may be recycled. The woman nods, though she looks disappointed.

“She wrote in them,” she says, taking out a guide to Italy. On the inside cover, in careful blue ink, is a list: *Rome, Florence, Siena, the sea.*

“Did she go?” Mara asks.

“Once. She came back and talked about it for twenty years.”

The woman opens the book to a photograph of a crowded square. In the margin her mother has written, *The bells were louder than I thought*. For a moment they both look at the words. Mara asks if the woman would like to keep this one. After some hesitation, she slips it into her bag. The rest she leaves on the desk.

By ten, the children’s room is busy. A toddler in a yellow coat has discovered that the rug contains pictures of animals and is trying to feed a wooden block to each one. His father follows at a discreet distance, retrieving the block when it rolls under furniture. At the low tables, two sisters are making signs for an imaginary shop. One writes *OPEN* in letters that occupy the entire page. The other writes *CLOSED*, then decorates it with so many flowers that the message seems less final.

The story-time librarian, who has learned that small children respond best to stories with repetition and a reasonable chance of making animal noises, begins reading about a bear who loses his hat. The children supply the animal noises even when the text does not call for them. Their parents sit on the floor, some joining in, others resting for a few minutes with the peculiar alertness of adults who know that peace can end suddenly.

Across the building, at a public computer, a man named Luis is trying to upload a résumé. He has the file on his phone but cannot remember the password for his email account. The application will close at five. He has already visited the employment office, where someone told him to use a computer at the library, and he has taken two buses to get here. When the password fails for the third time, he presses his palms against his eyes.

Mara cannot recover the password for him, but she can help him find another route. They connect his phone to the computer, locate the file, and save a copy to the desktop. The application form asks him to list each previous job separately, including the month he started and left. He calls his sister for help with one date. Mara moves away to give him privacy, then returns when he raises his hand. Forty minutes later, the application is submitted. Luis sits still for a few seconds, looking at the confirmation screen.

“Should I print it?” he asks.

“Yes,” Mara says. “Let’s print it.”

He folds the page and puts it carefully into his jacket pocket. He thanks her, and she tells him he did the difficult part. This is true, though the difficult part included asking for help in a room full of strangers, waiting through several small failures, and continuing when it would have been easy to leave. The confirmation page does not show any of that. It contains his name, a number, and the date.

At the reference desk, a teenager wants to know whether the library has books about mushrooms. She is especially interested in fungi that glow. Mara finds several titles, including one with photographs of luminous mushrooms clustered around a fallen branch. The girl studies the picture, then asks whether the light is bright enough to read by. Mara does not know. They look it up together and find an account by a researcher who tried, with difficulty, to read text by the light of several specimens. The girl borrows the book and photographs the page about bioluminescence.

By noon, rain has begun. People arrive with wet shoulders and newspapers held over their heads. A courier delivers a plastic crate of books requested from other branches: a history of bridge construction, a novel in large print, a cookbook devoted to beans, and a guide to repairing old bicycles. Each book has a slip of paper tucked inside bearing the name of the person who asked for it. Mara scans the barcodes and places the books on the hold shelf. Later, their borrowers will receive messages telling them the books are ready.

The hold shelf is one of Mara’s favorite places in the building. It gives her fleeting glimpses of projects already underway: someone is planning a garden, someone wants to learn Portuguese, someone needs a book about caring for a parent with dementia. Sometimes a person requests every volume in a long series and returns them within weeks, moving through a fictional world with an appetite Mara recognizes. She tries not to make stories out of the names and titles. People can surprise you, and a book about beekeeping might be research for a painting.

The rain grows heavier, and the windows turn gray. At a table by the periodicals, a man in a delivery uniform eats crackers from a paper sleeve while studying a map on his phone. Eating is not technically allowed in that part of the library. Mara sees him, sees the rain on his sleeves, and decides that the crackers are unlikely to cause trouble. She makes a mental note to check the floor after he leaves. He brushes the crumbs into his hand before standing up, then thanks her for letting him stay.

In the afternoon, a class from the nearby school arrives for a lesson on finding reliable information. The students are old enough to be skeptical and young enough to enjoy catching an adult in a mistake. Mara shows them a webpage claiming that a certain animal can live for hundreds of years. She asks what they would want to check before believing it. One student suggests looking for the author. Another says to compare the claim with a museum or university website. A third points out that the page is trying to sell an expensive supplement.

They investigate the animal and discover that the original claim has been exaggerated. The students are pleased. Mara is pleased too, though she knows the lesson will not solve every problem they encounter online. Next week they may see a misleading video shared by someone they trust, or a true story presented without enough context. Still, they have practiced pausing. They have learned that a confident sentence can be examined, and that changing their minds after finding better evidence is a useful skill rather than an embarrassment.

After the class leaves, Mara finds a pencil drawing on one of the tables. It depicts a dragon curled around a stack of books, wearing what appear to be glasses. Beneath it, the artist has written, *DO NOT DISTURB. RESEARCH IN PROGRESS.* There is no name. Mara puts the drawing on the staff-room noticeboard, next to the schedule and a reminder about the fire drill. By the end of the week, someone has added a speech bubble: *Unless you have snacks.*

The library keeps many records. It tracks loans, returns, attendance, computer sessions, and the number of questions answered at the desk. These figures help the staff request funding and show which services people use. They also help reveal practical problems. If the computers are occupied from morning to evening, perhaps more are needed. If a branch’s visitors have increased while its hours have stayed the same, the schedule may need another look.

Other things are harder to record. The staff know that an older visitor comes in on Tuesdays because his apartment is too quiet. They know that a student sometimes waits in the library until her mother finishes work. They know which children are proud to have their own cards and which adults are embarrassed to ask for help with a basic task. The staff cannot put all of this into a spreadsheet, and much of it is private. They carry it instead as part of their knowledge of the building and the people who use it.

Around three, Mr. Bell returns. He has left his scarf on the chair where he read the newspapers. Mara retrieves it from the lost-and-found shelf and hands it over.

“I thought it was gone for good,” he says.

“It was enjoying the company of an umbrella and a mitten.”

He looks at the shelf. “That umbrella won’t do much in this weather.”

“No,” Mara says. “Its owner may have discovered that already.”

Mr. Bell wraps the scarf around his neck. At the door he pauses to examine the noticeboard, where the library has posted a schedule of upcoming events: a local history talk, a sewing group, a workshop on tenant rights, and a Saturday session where volunteers will help people repair small household items. He takes a flyer for the history talk. On his way out, he asks whether there will be tea. Mara says she will find out.

The local history talk was arranged after a volunteer found a box of photographs in a cupboard at the community center. The photographs show the town across several decades: a parade with homemade floats, a row of shops before the road was widened, a group of children standing beside a newly planted tree. Many have names written on the back, but some do not. At the event, the organizers hope visitors will recognize a face, a storefront, or a year.

Mara has seen a few of the photographs. In one, a woman stands outside a bakery holding a tray of bread. Her expression is serious, but there is flour on the end of her nose. Behind her, someone has propped the door open with a crate. Mara likes the picture because so much of the workday remains visible in it: the tray has been brought out to cool, the door has been opened, and the photographer has caught the baker before she has had time to wipe her face.

At four, the teenager interested in mushrooms comes back to the desk. She has found another book, this one about forests, and wants to know whether she can borrow both. Mara checks her account. There is a small overdue fine from a book returned months earlier. The girl’s expression changes when she hears about it. She opens her purse and counts coins onto the counter.

Mara explains that the library recently removed overdue fines for children and teenagers. The old charge should have been cleared. She fixes the account, and the girl puts her coins away.

“I thought I couldn’t use my card,” she says.

“You can,” Mara tells her. “And you can take both books.”

The girl leaves with the books held against her chest. Mara wonders how long she has been staying away. There is no way to know, and she does not ask. She makes a note to mention the problem at the next staff meeting, in case other old charges have been missed.

The rain stops shortly before closing. A pale light comes through the windows, showing fingerprints on the glass and the tracks people have made across the entrance mat. The staff begin their final round. They collect books left on tables, push in chairs, and check the rooms at the back. In the children’s area, the wooden block has been placed carefully on the picture of a lion. One of the sisters has left her flower-covered *CLOSED* sign beside the shelves. Mara sets it on the desk in case she returns for it.

The last visitors gather their things. Luis’s computer has been used by three other people since he printed his confirmation page. The newspapers have been folded and refolded. The mushroom books are gone, as is the guide to repairing bicycles. A woman picks up the cookbook about beans and tells Mara she is trying to cook more cheaply. At the door, she flips through it and finds a recipe she wants to make that evening.

Once everyone has left, the building begins to sound like itself again. The cart bumps over the seam between carpet and tile. A printer, finally idle, clicks as it cools. Mara checks the lost-and-found shelf before turning off the lights. The scarf is gone, but the mitten remains. She moves it to the front, where it will be easy to see in the morning.

Outside, the pavement reflects the traffic lights. The buses are running late after the rain, and a small group has gathered beneath the shelter across the street. Mara locks the door and tests the handle. Through the glass she can see the return slot, already holding a book someone has slipped inside. She will check it in tomorrow. For now, she pulls up her hood and walks toward the bus stop, passing a puddle in which the library windows shine for a few more minutes before the lights switch off.

# The Things We Keep Working

The repair shop stood between a shuttered bakery and a building that had once sold shoes. Its window was full of objects nobody had collected: a brass clock with no hands, a red kettle, a violin case with a broken clasp. Above them hung a sign that said **VALE REPAIRS**, although the gold letters had faded so badly that, in certain weather, it seemed to say only **REPAIRS**.

Mara Vale had not been inside for eleven years when her father died. She had visited him, certainly: dinners at the little restaurant near the station, afternoons in his apartment, one uncomfortable Christmas at her place in the city. But the shop had remained outside those visits, like a subject both of them had agreed not to discuss.

She arrived on a Monday carrying a suitcase, a folder of legal documents, and a set of keys she had taken from his kitchen drawer. The largest key turned reluctantly. When the door opened, a small bell rang overhead, and she was surprised by how much she resented the sound. It was cheerful in the same old way, as though her father might appear from the back room and say, “Morning, love. You’re early.”

The shop smelled of metal filings, furniture polish, and the faintly sweet dust that gathers around old paper. Tools hung above the workbench in outlines her father had drawn with a marker: pliers, screwdrivers, a hammer with a handle worn smooth. There were jars of screws sorted by size and a radio with its back removed. A calendar on the wall showed a lake beneath mountains. It was still turned to March, although it was nearly June.

Mara opened the windows. Outside, a delivery truck reversed with a patient electronic warning. Across the street, two workers were measuring the front of the old cinema, which had been bought by a development company. The company had also expressed interest in her father’s building. Its representative had called twice in the week since the funeral, using the careful voice people adopt when they want to make an offer without appearing to have arrived too soon.

Her plan was straightforward. She would inventory the shop, contact the owners of anything valuable, donate what could be donated, and sell the building. She had taken five days off work, and five days ought to be enough. The company would turn the row into apartments with shops on the ground floor. The drawings showed large windows, pale brick, and trees that looked very healthy.

On the counter lay her father’s ledger. He had used it to record repairs, though he also kept a computer under the bench. Mara had bought him the computer seven years earlier. He had thanked her and then spent an entire afternoon asking it questions in a tone of mounting suspicion. She was pleased to see that he had eventually learned to use it. The ledger, however, was clearly where he put the details he cared about.

“Blue lamp, Mrs. Chen,” one entry read. “Cord frayed near base. Call before replacing shade.”

Another said: “Record player. Customer says it slows down when sad songs come on. Could not reproduce condition, but belt is stretched.”

Mara smiled despite herself. Farther down the page, her father had written: “Green chair. Do not touch until I find the right wood.”

There was no customer’s name beside that entry, just a date from six months earlier. Mara looked around the shop and spotted the chair in the corner. It was a child’s chair, painted a green so deep it appeared almost black. One leg was missing. Its seat had been scratched with the letters **J. R.**, and a small carved bird perched at the top of the backrest.

She moved it away from the wall. The carving was crude but lively; the bird’s beak was a little too long, and one wing was larger than the other. Whoever had made it had left tiny marks in the wood around the feathers. Her father would have noticed those marks. He used to run his thumb over old furniture and tell her where the maker had changed their mind.

At ten o’clock, someone knocked on the open door. A woman in a raincoat stood outside holding a paper bag against her chest.

“I saw the window open,” she said. “I’m sorry. I heard about your dad.”

Mara thanked her. The woman introduced herself as Mrs. Chen and asked whether there was any chance her lamp had been finished. She seemed embarrassed to ask, so Mara looked it up in the ledger and found it beneath the counter, wrapped in newspaper. Her father had attached a tag that said **DONE** and included the price.

Mrs. Chen unwrapped it carefully. The lamp had a ceramic base painted with pears. She plugged it into the socket by the door, and a soft yellow light came on beneath the old shade.

“He said I should keep the shade if I could,” she said. “It was my mother’s. I thought it looked too worn.”

“It looks nice,” Mara said.

“I think so too.” Mrs. Chen paid in cash, then lingered. “Is the shop closing?”

“Yes. I’m sorting everything out this week.”

Mrs. Chen nodded. She looked toward the workbench, where a pair of glasses lay beside a small tin of screws. “He used to call me when he got stuck on the crossword. I never knew why he thought I’d be any good. Half the time I had to ask my husband.”

After she left, Mara wrote **COLLECTED** beside the lamp in the ledger. She liked the neatness of it. By noon she had found owners for a toaster, two watches, and an electric fan. She made a list of phone numbers and began calling. Some people thanked her. One had forgotten about the item entirely. Another said he had moved away and told her to keep his broken camera.

The chair remained unexplained. Mara searched the ledger again, then the computer, where her father had created a folder called CUSTOMERS and filled it with documents named things like “new list” and “new list proper.” In one file she found an entry for a chair with “bird on back,” but the name field was blank. The phone number had only five digits.

That afternoon, a boy came in with a portable speaker that no longer charged. Mara explained that the shop was closing and that she did not know how to fix it.

“You could probably get a new one for less than a repair,” she said.

“I know,” he replied. “But this one was a present.”

He looked perhaps fourteen. One corner of the speaker had been held together with tape. Mara thought of the apartments she designed at her firm, the immaculate renderings where every surface was clear and every object appeared to have been chosen on purpose. The boy’s speaker would not have survived the first round of revisions.

“There’s another repair place near the station,” she said. “They might be able to help.”

He nodded, but he did not leave immediately. He looked at the green chair. “My grandma has one like that.”

“Does she?”

“Not green. Hers is blue. It has a cat on it.”

Mara asked his grandmother’s name. He told her it was Ruth James and gave her an address on Bell Street.

The house on Bell Street was small and impeccably maintained. A ceramic frog sat by the door, holding a sign that said **WELCOME, SORT OF**. Mara rang the bell and heard a dog bark from somewhere deep inside. After a minute, the door opened, and a woman in a cardigan looked at her over the top of her glasses.

“I’m sorry to bother you,” Mara began. “My name is Mara Vale. My father owned the repair shop.”

“I remember you,” the woman said. “You used to draw on his invoices.”

Mara had no memory of this, but she believed it. As a child she had spent whole Saturdays under the counter with pencils, drawing houses full of staircases that led nowhere. Her father had let her stay there as long as she didn’t touch the sharp tools or eat the washers.

Mrs. James invited her in. In the sitting room, a blue child’s chair stood beside the fireplace, a carved cat curled along its backrest. It was unmistakably related to the green chair. The proportions were the same; so were the uneven little marks around the carving.

“My grandfather made four of them,” Mrs. James said. “One for each of his grandchildren. Mine, my sister’s, and two for our cousins.”

“Do you know who might have the green one?”

“That was my sister’s. Jean.” Mrs. James touched the back of the blue chair. “She died in January.”

Mara apologized and explained that the chair was still at the shop. Mrs. James seemed puzzled. She knew her sister had broken a leg off the chair, but she had not known where it had gone.

“Jean’s son cleared her house,” she said. “He lives in Scotland now. I don’t suppose he remembered it was being repaired.”

She gave Mara his number. Before Mara left, Mrs. James showed her a photograph of the four cousins sitting on their chairs in a garden, their knees pressed together, their expressions solemn. The chairs had been freshly painted. The bird on Jean’s chair was not green but yellow, and the cat on Ruth’s was white.

“Granddad made them from whatever he could find,” Mrs. James said. “An old table, bits of a wardrobe. The seats were all different underneath.”

Back at the shop, Mara tipped the green chair onto its side. The underside of the seat was unpainted. There was a dark line where two pieces of wood had been joined, and a penciled measurement, still visible after all those years. Her father had left the broken leg on a shelf above the bench. It had split near the joint, and someone—perhaps Jean—had tried to glue it back together.

Mara called Jean’s son, Peter. He answered from a train and asked her to call again the next evening. She put the chair beside the workbench, intending to leave it alone. But later, while sorting a drawer, she found a piece of wood with a note attached in her father’s handwriting: **For the green chair? Check grain.**

She held it against the broken leg. The color was close, though not exact. She could imagine him examining it, deciding it was promising, setting it aside for a quieter day. He had been ill for longer than he admitted. Perhaps he had meant to return the chair before going into the hospital. Perhaps he had simply forgotten.

Mara found a notebook beside the wood. Most of its pages held measurements, sketches, and reminders to order parts. Near the back was a drawing of the chair leg, with arrows indicating where to cut. Her father had even written down the size of the drill bit he intended to use.

She had not repaired anything made of wood since she was seventeen. That summer, she and her father had built shelves for her bedroom. He insisted on measuring each wall twice, and she insisted that he was taking too long. When the shelves were done, one tilted slightly. She had blamed him. Years later she realized the floor was uneven, but by then there seemed no useful occasion to mention it.

On Tuesday morning she called her office and said she might need an extra day. Then she took the broken leg, the new piece of wood, and the notebook into the back room. The saw was heavier than she remembered. She practiced on a scrap first, making a cut that wandered badly. Her second cut was better. By lunchtime she had produced something that looked roughly like a chair leg, though it was thicker at one end.

She was sanding it when someone cleared his throat in the doorway. It was the boy with the speaker.

“My grandma said you came by,” he said. “She sent these.”

He handed her a container of biscuits and watched her work. After a moment he said, “That’s not straight.”

“I know.”

“My dad has a machine for that.”

“What kind of machine?”

“I don’t know. It makes things straight.”

His father turned out to be a cabinetmaker named Daniel, who worked from a shed behind his house. He came by after school, examined the leg, and agreed that Mara’s father’s piece of wood was a good match. He also pointed out that Mara had cut it the wrong way against the grain.

“Will it break?” she asked.

“Not necessarily. But I’d start again.”

He showed her how to mark the wood and offered to make the leg at his workshop. Mara almost accepted. Then she remembered the measurements in the notebook and asked if he could show her how to do it instead. Daniel looked at his watch, considered, and pulled up a stool.

They worked for two hours. He did the difficult cut, but Mara shaped the taper and drilled the hole for the joint. When she fitted the leg to the chair, it sat slightly proud of the frame. Daniel showed her where to pare it back. They tested the fit again and again, taking off a little each time, until the leg met the seat cleanly.

The glue needed to dry overnight. Daniel advised her not to paint it until she had checked that the chair was steady. As he left, he noticed the shelf of uncollected objects in the window.

“What happens to all those?” he asked.

“I’m not sure yet.”

“My son would take half of them if you let him. He’s always bringing things home to pull apart.”

On Wednesday, Peter called. He remembered the chair at once. His mother had kept it in her hallway with a pot of flowers on the seat. When the leg broke, she had refused to throw it away, but she had not mentioned taking it to be repaired.

“I’m glad it’s there,” he said. “I thought it had gone with the rest of the furniture.”

Mara told him about the new leg and offered to send the chair when it was finished. He thanked her, then said, “Actually, would you mind if my aunt kept it for now? I’m in the middle of moving again, and she knew how much Mum liked it.”

Mrs. James was delighted when Mara called. She came to the shop that afternoon and sat on a stool while Mara painted the leg. The new green did not match perfectly. The old paint had darkened and collected tiny scratches over decades; the new paint was smooth and bright.

“I could paint the whole chair,” Mara said.

“Please don’t. I like being able to see what’s happened to it.”

While the paint dried, they drank tea from mismatched mugs. Mrs. James told Mara that her father had repaired the blue chair too, years ago, after her grandson stood on it to reach a shelf. He had charged her very little and then borrowed the chair for a week, wanting to study how it had been made.

“He asked if my grandfather had been a carpenter,” she said. “He hadn’t. He worked at the docks. Your father seemed pleased about that.”

“Why?”

“I think he liked knowing the chairs were made at home.”

On Thursday, Mara met the development company’s representative. He wore a good coat and carried the drawings in a cardboard tube. He walked through the shop, speaking about timelines, structural surveys, and the advantages of agreeing before construction costs rose again. His offer was fair. Mara had checked it with a lawyer and with a friend who knew the local market.

She asked what would happen to the shops in the new building.

“They’ll be available to rent,” he said.

“At the current rates?”

He gave her a sympathetic look. “We can’t promise that.”

After he left, Mara sat at the counter with the offer in front of her. She did not want to run a repair shop. She liked her job, her apartment, and the friends she had made in the city. She had spent years building a life that fit her, and she had no wish to abandon it because she felt guilty about a building.

But she also thought of Daniel’s son, Mrs. Chen’s lamp, and the objects waiting in the window. Her father had owned the building outright. That gave her options she had not considered on Monday.

She called Daniel and asked whether he knew anyone who might want the space. By Friday afternoon he had introduced her to a woman who repaired bicycles and a man who restored old radios. Neither could afford the whole shop. Together, they thought they might manage it, especially if Daniel rented the back room for overflow work.

They walked through the building with Mara, discussing shelves, insurance, and where a bicycle stand might fit. Their ideas were practical and occasionally contradictory. The radio restorer wanted less dust; Daniel wanted a larger saw. The bicycle mechanic pointed out that the front door was too narrow for some cargo bikes. They agreed to get estimates before making any promises.

It would take longer than five days to settle. There were permits to check and a lease to write. Mara called her office again and arranged to work remotely for the following week. She also called the development company and told them she was not ready to sell.

On Saturday morning, Mrs. James came to collect the green chair. She had brought Peter’s old baby blanket to wrap around it for the journey home. Mara set the chair on the pavement so they could inspect it in daylight. The new leg held firm. The paint was still a shade too bright, but the carved bird looked down over it with its lopsided wings.

Mrs. James ran her hand across the seat. “Jean used to sit on this with her feet tucked underneath her,” she said. “She’d insist she wasn’t getting in anyone’s way, even when she was right in the middle of the room.”

She smiled and wrapped the blanket around the chair. Mara carried it to her car and fastened the seat belt around it. When she closed the door, the chair remained upright, facing forward as though it had somewhere important to be.

Back in the shop, the bell rang behind her. She looked at the workbench and saw that she had left her father’s glasses beside the tin of screws. She picked them up and folded them carefully. Then she opened a drawer, found an empty case, and put them inside.

There were still calls to make, shelves to clear, and an old radio waiting for someone who knew what to do with it. Mara took the ledger from the counter, turned to a clean page, and began writing down the names of the people who had offered to help.

samples.result:
# The Quiet Work of Keeping Things Going

On a street I once imagined, there is a clock above the door of a bakery. Its face is cream-colored, its hands are black, and it has been five minutes slow for as long as anyone can remember. The baker knows this. The people who buy bread know it too. A child once asked why nobody fixed it, and the baker said that everyone had simply learned to make the adjustment. This is one way a community forms: not always through agreement about what is true, but through shared knowledge of a small, persistent error.

Eventually, though, the clock stops altogether. The baker notices because the morning customers arrive, the ovens grow hot, the first loaves go into paper bags, and the hands remain where they were. She takes the clock down after closing and sets it on the counter. It is heavier than she expected. Dust has gathered along its upper edge, where no one standing below could see. She opens the back, replaces the battery, and waits. The second hand moves. Then she sets the correct time, hangs the clock up again, and goes home.

The next morning, several people are late.

They have not become less punctual overnight. They have merely lost an adjustment they had practiced so often that they no longer knew they were making it. A clock that was wrong in a familiar way had become part of their sense of the morning. Now it is right, and for a few days the street must relearn it. Someone jokes that the baker ought to put it back. She refuses, though she admits she almost did. By the following week, most customers have adapted. One man continues to arrive five minutes early and discovers that he likes having time to talk.

I keep returning to this imaginary clock because it suggests that maintenance is rarely as simple as restoring an object to an ideal state. Things settle into relationships with the people who use them. A door that sticks teaches the household to lift its handle. A bus that consistently arrives late changes when passengers leave home. A computer with an unreliable key produces a population of elaborate workarounds. Repairing the object can be a relief, but it can also disturb habits that have grown around its defect. Even a good change asks something of the people who live with it.

The word “maintenance” has an unglamorous sound. It suggests forms, schedules, grease, invoices, and rooms entered only when something has gone wrong. We tend to celebrate the opening of a bridge rather than the inspections that allow it to remain open decades later. We photograph a freshly painted school, not the person who returns each evening to clean its floors. Yet most of the built world exists because someone repeatedly performs tasks that leave little visible trace. The better those tasks are done, the easier they are to overlook.

There is a particular kind of skill in noticing what has not yet failed. A gardener sees that one branch is rubbing against another and ties it back before the bark is damaged. A mechanic hears a faint change in an engine and knows where to look. A teacher recognizes that a student’s sudden silence may be worth a gentle question. Such attention is not clairvoyance. It is often the accumulated result of looking at ordinary things for a long time, learning their patterns, and taking small deviations seriously without assuming every deviation is a disaster.

Not every problem can be prevented, of course. Some failures arrive without warning, and some systems have been neglected for so long that a modest repair cannot make them sound. Preventive work is also vulnerable to a strange accounting problem: when it succeeds, the avoided trouble may be difficult to prove. A repaired roof that does not leak provides less dramatic evidence than a bucket placed beneath a drip. It takes trust, records, and institutional memory to value the dry room as an achievement rather than merely the natural condition of a room.

A person who maintains a library knows this. Books return with loosened bindings, torn pages, mysterious stains, and bookmarks made from receipts, photographs, and grocery lists. Computers need updates. Heating systems fail. A chair develops a wobble that becomes more pronounced with every person who sits in it. None of this is the library’s central purpose, yet the purpose depends on it. A library cannot lend books that have fallen apart or welcome people into rooms that are unsafe. Care for the physical setting makes quieter forms of care possible.

Maintenance also reveals how much knowledge is local. A building may have a manual, but the person who has worked there for twenty years knows which window lets in rain when the wind comes from the east. A cook knows that one burner runs hotter than the others. A ferry captain knows where the current behaves oddly after heavy rain. This knowledge can be recorded, and it should be shared, but it often begins in the body: in repeated movements, close observation, and the gradual refinement of judgment.

There is a risk in romanticizing this expertise. The person who knows every weakness in a building may also be the person carrying an unreasonable workload because no one has funded proper repairs. A neighborhood’s ingenuity in coping with unreliable services is not a substitute for reliable services. Adaptation deserves respect, but the need to adapt can be evidence of neglect. The baker’s slow clock is a harmless inconvenience; the same cannot be said of every broken thing people learn to work around.

Some repairs are easy to recognize because they return an object to its earlier function. A torn coat is stitched, a punctured tire is patched, a lamp gets a new switch. Others change the object in the process. A ramp added to an old entrance does not merely restore the building; it makes the building available to people who may previously have been excluded. A safer street crossing does more than replace worn paint. It changes who can move through a place with confidence. Sometimes keeping something useful means refusing to preserve it exactly as it was.

The difference matters when people argue about whether a place is being maintained or transformed. A town may want to preserve an old public square. But which version of the square should it preserve? The one with uneven stones that some residents love and others cannot cross safely? The one with mature trees whose roots now threaten the paving? The one remembered by people who grew up nearby, or the one used today by people who arrived later? These questions do not have answers hidden in the original blueprint. They require negotiation among living people.

The same is true of traditions. A recipe survives because someone cooks it, but also because someone substitutes an ingredient, adjusts the heat, or writes down an instruction that was once passed along by watching. A song survives because it is sung in voices different from those that first carried it. A language survives through speakers who use it to discuss new objects and unfamiliar experiences. Repetition alone is not enough. What lasts must be made usable again and again, often by people whose circumstances the original makers could not have imagined.

This does not mean every change is automatically an improvement. A familiar shop can be renovated so thoroughly that it loses the qualities that made people care about it. A software update can solve one problem while making a common task harder. A family recipe can be simplified until the result no longer tastes like anything anyone remembers. Good maintenance requires some judgment about what must remain recognizable. That judgment is rarely perfect, but it begins by asking what people value before deciding what is obsolete.

I think of an old wooden table with a ring left by a glass. If the table is stripped and refinished, the ring may disappear. Whether that is desirable depends partly on what the ring means. Perhaps it is an ugly mark on a surface the owner wants to use for formal dinners. Perhaps it was left during a long conversation with someone who has since died. The mark is physically the same in either case. Its significance belongs to the life around it, and a restorer who ignores that life may polish away something important.

There is also pleasure in keeping things going. Sharpening a pencil with a small knife, oiling a bicycle chain, darning a sock, or washing a favorite cup can be satisfying because the connection between effort and result is visible. Many forms of work offer no such clarity. A person may send messages all day and end the afternoon unsure what has changed. A cleaned window, by contrast, admits the light differently. This modest satisfaction should not be confused with a universal solution to modern discontent, but it is real.

Repair can alter our sense of an object’s history. A patched jacket is no longer merely the jacket that tore; it is also the jacket that someone decided was worth mending. A ceramic bowl joined after breaking carries a visible record of an accident and a response to it. The repair may be inelegant. The stitches may be uneven, the glue line obvious. Still, the object has acquired evidence of attention. It has been seen at the moment when throwing it away would have been easiest, and someone chose otherwise.

Yet keeping everything is not always wise. Objects consume space and time. An appliance may use so much energy that replacing it is sensible. A chair may be beyond safe repair. A coat may no longer fit anyone who could use it. The moral drama sometimes attached to possessions can make ordinary decisions feel heavier than they need to be. Care includes knowing when to let go, how to dispose of something responsibly when possible, and how to avoid making a shrine of every item that once served a purpose.

People, too, can become exhausted by the demand to maintain. There is always another meal to make, another message to answer, another appointment to arrange. Much of this work happens in households, where it can be difficult to see because it is scattered across the day. Someone notices that soap is running low, remembers a birthday, replaces a dead battery, and checks whether a child has shoes that fit. Each task is small. Together they form a substantial labor of anticipation, and the person doing it may receive attention only when something is missed.

Sharing that labor requires more than offering help after being asked. It requires learning to notice what needs doing and taking responsibility for the whole task. Buying groceries, for example, may include noticing what is missing, considering what people will eat, making a list, going to the shop, putting things away, and remembering that a particular ingredient will spoil quickly. If one person must supervise every step, the work has not really been shared. A well-maintained household depends not only on effort but on distributing the burden of attention.

Friendships need attention of a different kind. There are friendships that can withstand years of silence and resume easily, but even these usually depend on some earlier investment of trust. Most relationships are sustained through smaller acts: sending a message, remembering a difficult week, making an invitation, apologizing without turning the apology into a defense. Such acts do not guarantee closeness. People change, and not every relationship can or should continue. Still, affection that is never expressed can become difficult for another person to distinguish from absence.

Institutions face a similar challenge at a larger scale. A public promise means little if there is no process for carrying it out, no one with authority to respond when it fails, and no way for affected people to be heard. Trust is not maintained by declarations alone. It grows when a school communicates honestly with families, when a hospital explains an error, when a government agency answers a complaint, or when an employer corrects a problem without waiting for public embarrassment. These actions are often slow and administratively dull. Their consequences are not.

There is a temptation to divide people into builders and maintainers, as though creation were one temperament and care another. In practice, the same person may do both. The engineer designing a bridge must imagine how it will be inspected and repaired. The parent inventing a bedtime story is also maintaining a ritual. The gardener who plants a tree makes something possible that years of watering and pruning will support. Creation is not a single moment followed by an unrelated period of upkeep. It is often an invitation to a longer relationship.

That relationship extends into the future, where its participants are mostly unknown to us. Someone planted trees whose shade now falls on sidewalks they never walked. Someone preserved documents that later readers would need for reasons the preservers could not have predicted. Someone maintained a water system through a season when almost nobody thought about it. We inherit the results of countless decisions made by people who did not know our names. We also leave behind the results of our own attention and inattention.

At the bakery, the clock is still keeping good time. The regular customers have stopped commenting on it, and the man who began arriving early sometimes holds the door for others. None of this is a grand achievement. The battery will eventually run down again, the hands will stop, and the baker or someone else will have to take the clock from the wall. That future task does not make the present repair meaningless. It is simply part of what it means for a useful thing to last: not that it escapes the need for care, but that care is offered more than once.

# The Department of Small Repairs

When the town council announced that it was closing the Department of Small Repairs, most people assumed it was a joke.

The department occupied a narrow room behind the post office. Its window displayed a clock that had stopped at twenty past three, a blue ceramic bird with one wing glued back on, and a handwritten sign that said:

**IF IT CAN BE MENDED, WE WILL TRY.  
IF IT CANNOT, WE WILL TELL YOU GENTLY.**

The clock had not been left there as an advertisement. It belonged to the department’s only employee, a woman named Mara, who had been meaning to fix it for eleven years.

For nearly four decades, residents had brought her objects that were broken but not, in their owners’ judgment, finished: umbrellas that would not open, lamps that would not light, drawers that refused to remain closed. Mara repaired these things when she could. When she could not, she often found them a second life. A teapot with a cracked spout became a planter. A wooden ladder with one missing rung became a shelf for shoes.

The department charged according to an old schedule taped beside the door. Most prices were absurdly low. A loose button cost twenty cents. A bicycle bell cost fifty. Anything requiring more than an hour was listed as “to be discussed,” which usually meant Mara would accept a jar of jam, a ride to the hardware store, or nothing at all.

The council called it an inefficient use of public funds. A neighboring town, the mayor pointed out, had replaced its repair service with a website listing private contractors.

“How many people actually use it?” he asked at the meeting.

The finance clerk checked her notes. “Last year, four hundred and twelve visits.”

“Out of a population of eight thousand.”

“Yes.”

The mayor nodded, as if the number settled the matter. The room was nearly empty. Nobody spoke against the proposal, and the department was scheduled to close at the end of September.

Mara learned about the decision from a printed notice slipped beneath her door.

She read it twice, put it under the blue bird, and went back to work on a toaster.

---

The first person she told was a boy named Ivo, who came in every Thursday after school with his grandmother’s shopping cart. The cart had a squeaking wheel that Mara had repaired six times. Each repair lasted a few weeks before the squeak returned.

“You’re closing?” Ivo asked.

“Apparently.”

“Where will the things go?”

“Some will go home. The tools belong to the council, so I suppose they’ll go into storage.”

“I meant the things people bring.”

Mara considered this. “I suppose people will have to find someone else.”

Ivo looked around the room. On the counter sat a radio with its back removed, a purse missing a clasp, and a green watering can with a hole near the handle. Above them hung a photograph of the town’s old railway station, which had been demolished before he was born.

“Who else can fix all this?”

“There are people who know more than I do about most things in here,” Mara said. “They’re just harder to find.”

She turned the cart upside down and examined its wheel. Ivo had wrapped the axle in a strip of blue cloth, which was already fraying.

“Was this your repair?”

He nodded.

“It was worth trying.”

“It didn’t work.”

“It worked for a while.”

“That’s not the same.”

“No,” Mara said. “But it’s not nothing.”

She removed the cloth, cleaned the axle, and fitted a small washer from a tin beneath the counter. When she set the cart upright, it rolled silently across the floor.

Ivo pushed it back and forth. “How long will it last?”

“I don’t know. If it starts squeaking again, bring it before September.”

He left with the cart and returned ten minutes later without it.

“Can I help you stay open?” he asked.

Mara was searching for a screw she had dropped. “You can help me find that first.”

They found it beneath the radiator.

---

Ivo’s grandmother, Mrs. Bell, said the council had made up its mind and that petitions rarely changed anything. Nevertheless, she signed the petition Ivo wrote, then took it to the bakery.

The baker signed because Mara had repaired the latch on his back gate. A woman buying rye bread signed because Mara had shortened the strap on her father’s medical bag after he died, so she could carry it herself. The baker’s apprentice signed because he liked Ivo, although he had never visited the department.

By the end of the week, the petition had thirty-seven names.

Ivo brought it to Mara, expecting approval. She read every name, including one that had been crossed out and rewritten because its owner had misspelled his own surname.

“Thank you,” she said.

“Is thirty-seven enough?”

“I doubt it.”

“How many do we need?”

“I don’t know that either.”

She pinned the petition beside the price list. The next morning, a man collecting his repaired lamp added his name. Later, a woman came in specifically to sign and stayed for twenty minutes, telling Mara about a music box she had owned as a child.

Mara listened, though she was unsure what the woman wanted from her. At last the woman took the music box from her handbag. It was small and pale green, painted with roses.

“It stopped years ago,” she said. “I thought perhaps you could look.”

The spring was broken. Mara did not have a replacement, and the mechanism was delicate enough that she was reluctant to improvise. She told the woman she would ask around.

The woman seemed disappointed, but she signed the petition before leaving.

That evening Mara telephoned a retired watchmaker in the next town. He knew where she might order a spring, though he warned her it could take months to arrive.

“Months might be too long,” Mara said.

“Then give them my number,” he replied.

---

As news of the closure spread, the department became busier than it had been in years. Some people came because they wanted a repair before the service disappeared. Others came because they wanted to see the place they had heard about and found something to bring with them.

A man arrived with a wooden duck whose head had fallen off. A schoolteacher brought a globe that had stopped turning on its stand. A teenager brought a cassette player she had bought at a market, along with a tape labeled **SUMMER 1998**.

“My mother made it,” she explained. “She says she doesn’t remember what’s on it.”

The cassette player needed a new belt. Mara ordered one and, while they waited, lent the girl an old player from the cupboard.

The girl returned the next day with a list of songs she and her mother had identified. There were two they could not name. At the end of the tape, after a long silence, they had heard a dog barking and someone laughing very close to the microphone.

“Was it your mother?” Mara asked.

“I think so. She thinks it was my aunt.”

The girl played that part three times, hoping Mara could settle the question. Mara could not, but she enjoyed listening.

Not every repair went well. Mara broke the brittle plastic catch on a lunch box while trying to replace its hinge. She apologized to the owner, a little girl who had waited beside the counter through the entire procedure.

The girl examined the damage and began to cry. Her father told her he would buy her a new lunch box, which made her cry harder.

Mara offered to make a leather strap that would hold the lid shut. The girl did not answer. She took the lunch box home, and for two days Mara assumed she would not see it again.

On the third day, the girl returned with her father and asked whether the strap could be red.

---

At the council’s next meeting, Ivo stood up during the public comment period and presented the petition. It had two hundred and six signatures.

The mayor thanked him and said that the council appreciated the community’s affection for the department. He also explained that the town faced rising costs: the school roof needed work, the water pipes beneath Alder Street had to be replaced, and the fire station’s engine was due for an expensive inspection.

“We have to make choices,” he said.

Ivo had prepared a speech, but it depended on the mayor being unreasonable. Faced with the list of repairs, he lost his place.

“Couldn’t you close something else?” he asked.

“Possibly,” said the mayor. “What would you suggest?”

Ivo looked at the council members. Behind them hung framed photographs of previous mayors, all wearing the same serious expression.

“I don’t know,” he admitted.

Afterward, the finance clerk found him in the corridor and showed him the budget. The department’s largest expense was Mara’s salary. There was also rent for the room, electricity, insurance, and a small allowance for supplies.

“Could volunteers run it?” Ivo asked.

“They might,” the clerk said. “But someone would have to organize them, and the council would still need to decide who was responsible if something went wrong.”

She did not say it to discourage him. She wrote the questions on the back of an agenda and gave it to him to take home.

That evening, Ivo and his grandmother spread the budget across their kitchen table. Mrs. Bell knew how to keep accounts; she had done them for her brother’s plumbing business for twenty years. She also knew people who might be willing to volunteer.

“First,” she said, “we need to ask Mara whether she wants to keep doing this.”

“She does,” Ivo said.

“Let’s ask her anyway.”

---

Mara wanted the department to stay open, but she was less certain about her own future. She had been thinking about retirement for some time. Her hands ached in cold weather, and she had begun to turn away repairs involving very small screws.

“I thought I might leave next spring,” she told Mrs. Bell and Ivo. “I hadn’t told anyone yet.”

Ivo stared at her. “But then who would do it?”

“That’s what we need to find out.”

The three of them made a list of people with useful skills. Some were professionals who might donate an occasional hour. Others were hobbyists, retirees, or people who had once mentioned knowing how to sew, sharpen blades, or repair radios.

The baker’s apprentice knew how to mend bicycle tires. The retired watchmaker agreed to visit once a month, provided someone collected him from the bus station. The schoolteacher with the globe offered to keep records. A tailor named Arun said he could come on Wednesdays after closing his shop.

By the following week, they had twelve volunteers and a problem: only Mara had a key to the department, and the council had not agreed to let anyone else use it.

The finance clerk suggested they submit a proposal. Ivo imagined a single page with everyone’s names on it, but Mrs. Bell insisted on a proper budget, a schedule, and a plan for handling complaints.

“What sort of complaints?” Ivo asked.

“The lunch box, for one.”

“It got a strap.”

“After Mara broke it. Suppose the owner had wanted her to pay for a new one.”

Mara nodded. “That’s fair. We should explain the risks before we start.”

They spent three evenings writing the proposal. Ivo designed a sign-up sheet, then redesigned it after discovering that his first version had no space for telephone numbers. Mrs. Bell called the insurance company. Mara counted tools and made a list of those she owned personally.

When the document was finished, it was eleven pages long. Ivo thought it looked important enough to work.

---

The council considered the proposal in August. The volunteers offered to run the department three days a week. They requested use of the room and its existing equipment, along with enough funding to cover insurance, utilities, and basic supplies.

The mayor asked what would happen if the volunteers lost interest.

“We’ll review the arrangement after six months,” Mrs. Bell said. “If we can’t keep the hours we’ve promised, you can end it.”

A council member asked whether local repair businesses objected to a free public service. Arun, the tailor, attended the meeting to answer. He said the department had referred customers to him for years, especially when a garment needed more work than Mara could manage.

“I’m not worried about losing business,” he said. “I’m worried about people throwing away a good coat because the lining has come loose.”

Another council member questioned whether volunteers could safely repair electrical appliances. Mara agreed that they needed limits. They proposed inspecting lamps and radios but referring complicated electrical work to qualified technicians.

The discussion lasted an hour. Ivo counted each minute on the clock above the door. When the council finally voted, the proposal passed by four votes to three.

The department would remain open for a six-month trial.

Outside, Ivo expected Mara to cheer. Instead, she sat on a bench and took a long breath.

“Are you happy?” he asked.

“Yes,” she said. “I’m also thinking about everything we’ve promised to do by Monday.”

He sat beside her. After a moment, she smiled.

“You did well in there.”

“I only carried the papers.”

“You carried them to the right place.”

Mrs. Bell came out with the finance clerk, who had already begun discussing forms. The four of them walked back toward the post office together, talking about keys, storage, and where they might put a second worktable.

---

The trial began unevenly.

On the first Monday, three volunteers arrived at nine, but nobody had remembered to unlock the cupboard containing the extension cords. On Wednesday, Arun discovered that the sewing machine needed a part Mara had ordered in June and forgotten to collect. On Friday, a customer brought in a chair, and the volunteers spent fifteen minutes deciding whether furniture counted as a small repair.

“It depends on the chair,” Mara said when she arrived.

This chair needed two joints reglued. They took it.

The volunteers developed a system. Each object received a numbered tag and a short description of the problem. Owners signed a form acknowledging that repairs might fail. Anything valuable, dangerous, or beyond the volunteers’ abilities was referred elsewhere.

Some visitors disliked the forms. One man announced that he had never been asked to sign anything when Mara worked alone.

“That was probably my mistake,” Mara told him.

He signed.

The worktable filled quickly. There were coats with torn pockets, a chessboard missing two squares of veneer, a pair of binoculars with a loose eyepiece, and a toy train that moved only when pushed. The volunteers learned to leave notes for one another. At first the notes were cryptic:

**SPRING IN TIN. DO NOT LOSE.**

Later they became more useful:

**Music box: replacement spring ordered. Owner is Mrs. Denby. Please call when it arrives. Number in ledger.**

Ivo came after school to sort screws, greet customers, and sweep the floor. He also learned that sorting screws was harder than it sounded. A single jar could contain a dozen sizes that looked nearly identical until someone needed a particular one.

Mara showed him how to measure them and where to find the thread gauge. He made labels for the drawers, then corrected several after the watchmaker pointed out that he had mixed up millimeters and fractions of an inch.

---

In October, the replacement spring for Mrs. Denby’s music box arrived.

The watchmaker fitted it while Mara and Ivo watched. He worked slowly, using a magnifying lens and a pair of tweezers so fine that Ivo was afraid to breathe near them.

When the mechanism was assembled, the watchmaker wound the key. The box played a tune none of them recognized. It was slightly uneven, with one note that sounded softer than the others, but it played all the way through.

Mrs. Denby came the next morning. She opened the lid, listened, and began to hum. Then she stopped.

“I thought I remembered it,” she said.

She listened again. The tune did not change. Afterward, she told them that her sister used to keep the box on a shelf above their beds. Perhaps she had been remembering a song her sister sang, rather than the music in the box.

“Is your sister still nearby?” Mara asked.

“In Bristol.”

Mrs. Denby took out her telephone and called her. She held it close to the music box while the tune played. Her sister could hear it, though not very well, and promised to call back that evening from a quieter room.

Before leaving, Mrs. Denby placed the box carefully in her handbag. She offered to pay the watchmaker, who accepted the cost of the spring and a slice of the cake she had brought from home.

That afternoon, Ivo asked Mara whether she had known the repair would succeed.

“No.”

“Were you worried?”

“A little.”

“Because she’d waited so long?”

“And because the watchmaker might have broken something else while fitting the spring. Old mechanisms can be stubborn.”

“But it worked.”

“Yes,” Mara said. “We were lucky, and he was careful.”

---

By December, the department had enough volunteers to open an extra half day. The finance clerk visited to check the accounts and found them in good order, though Mrs. Bell had to explain three entries written in Ivo’s handwriting.

The council’s six-month review was still months away. Nobody knew whether the service would become permanent, but people had begun to speak about it without adding “if it stays open.”

Mara reduced her hours. On Tuesdays she went swimming. On some Thursdays she took a bus to the coast and walked along the promenade, stopping for soup at a café where the windows steamed in cold weather. She still came to the department twice a week, and sometimes on other days if someone called with a question.

One wet afternoon, she found Ivo standing beneath the blue bird with the stopped clock in his hands.

“Can I try?” he asked.

“You can, but it may not be a simple job.”

He opened the back under her supervision. Dust had collected around the mechanism, and one of the hands was loose. The clock also needed a new mainspring, which neither of them had in stock.

Ivo looked disappointed.

“We can order one,” Mara said.

They wrote down the measurements and put the clock back in the window. It remained at twenty past three through Christmas and most of January.

When the spring finally came, Ivo installed it with help from the watchmaker. He tightened the loose hand and polished the glass. Then he wound the clock and set it on the counter.

It ticked loudly enough for everyone in the room to hear.

For the rest of the day, people checked it against their telephones. At first it ran four minutes fast. Ivo adjusted the regulator, and by closing time it was only thirty seconds ahead.

He carried it to the window, where Mara helped him settle it between the blue bird and the sign. Outside, rainwater ran along the curb, carrying a paper receipt toward the drain. The baker passed with an umbrella, paused to wave, and continued up the street.

Inside, Ivo watched the clock for another minute. Its second hand moved steadily. He knew he would have to check it again tomorrow.
