The library in my neighborhood opens at ten, but the building begins its work long before that. At eight, someone switches on the lights behind the tall windows. At nine, a delivery truck leaves a plastic crate by the side door. By half past nine, people have gathered on the steps: a man with a folded newspaper, a woman pushing a stroller, two teenagers sharing headphones. They wait without much conversation. When the doors open, they enter with the calm determination of people who have somewhere important to be.

Inside, the air smells faintly of paper and carpet cleaner. There is a place for children, where the shelves are low and the furniture is bright. There is a place for study, where the tables have power outlets and everyone pretends not to notice when someone’s phone vibrates. Near the entrance, a display recommends books about gardening, though the weather outside suggests that nothing green could possibly survive. The recommendations change every few weeks. Someone has to decide what goes there, and I like to imagine the discussion.

The librarians seem to know where everything is, including things that aren’t books. They can find a tax form, a local history photograph, or the name of an author described only as “the one who wrote that blue book about a dog.” They help people print documents and sign into computers. They explain, patiently and repeatedly, why a particular password must contain both a number and a symbol. Their expertise is practical, wide-ranging, and often exercised under fluorescent lights while a queue forms at the desk.

I used to think of libraries mainly as warehouses for books. That was when I had a quiet room of my own and reliable internet access and a printer that usually worked. Even then, I borrowed books I couldn’t afford to buy. But it took me longer to notice how much else the building offered. A student could stay all afternoon without ordering a drink. An older person could read the news in a warm room. Someone between apartments could charge a phone and make calls without explaining their circumstances.

One winter, the heating failed in my apartment for three days. The landlord promised that someone was coming, then promised it again. On the second morning, I packed my laptop and went to the library. I found a seat near a window, took off my gloves, and stayed until closing. Nobody asked why I was there so long. I worked for a while, read a magazine, and listened to the soft noises of other people occupying the room. By the time I left, my hands had stopped aching.

I began to recognize the regulars. A man in a wool cap arrived most afternoons and read automotive manuals. A woman brought a notebook and copied recipes from cookbooks, sometimes photographing a page before returning the book to its shelf. Two brothers came in after school and competed to see who could finish his homework first. They argued over the results, usually quietly, though not always. I never learned most of their names. Still, after a while, I missed them on days when their usual seats were empty.

The building is not perfectly peaceful. The printer jams, and the computers are sometimes all occupied. Children run when they have been asked to walk. Once, an argument over a missing charger grew loud enough that a librarian had to intervene. There are also rules: food is restricted in some rooms, meeting spaces must be reserved, and popular books have waiting lists. These limits can be inconvenient. They are also part of how the place remains usable by people with different needs, schedules, and tolerances for noise.

My favorite part of visiting is returning a book through the slot beside the desk. It disappears with a satisfying clunk, and soon someone else will be able to take it home. I sometimes wonder what previous readers made of the books I borrow. Occasionally there is a clue: a receipt used as a bookmark, a penciled question mark in a margin, a pressed leaf that has turned brittle and brown. The librarians would probably prefer that borrowers didn’t leave things inside, so I remove them when I find them.

Last spring, the library held a repair afternoon in the meeting room. Volunteers brought tools, and residents brought lamps, radios, torn coats, and other things they hoped could be saved. I took a desk fan whose switch had become unreliable. A volunteer opened the casing, found a loose connection, and fixed it while explaining what he was doing. At the next table, someone was learning to sew a button back onto a jacket. The event lasted only a few hours, but for weeks afterward I noticed that fan whenever I turned it on.

The last time I visited, I checked out a novel and sat for a few minutes by the front window. Rain had started while I was inside, and people stood beneath the awning deciding whether to wait it out. A librarian crossed the room carrying a stack of returned books. The brothers were at their usual table, working through what looked like a math assignment. When the rain eased, I put my book in my bag and went home. I’ll be back in three weeks, if not sooner.

The town kept its library in a former railway station, which seemed appropriate. Both places existed to send people elsewhere. The trains had stopped arriving decades earlier, but the clock above the entrance still worked, and the long benches still faced the empty tracks. On rainy afternoons, children pressed their noses against the glass and imagined destinations beyond the weeds. Adults came for quieter reasons: warmth, a newspaper, an hour without anyone asking what they planned to do next. The librarian, Mara, understood that a useful building did not need to explain itself to everyone who stepped through its doors.

One October morning, a small wooden box appeared on the circulation desk. It had a slot in its lid and a handwritten label: QUESTIONS WITH NO URGENT ANSWERS. Mara did not know who had put it there. The cleaner denied responsibility, and the volunteers looked genuinely puzzled. Still, the box was neatly made, and the label seemed harmless. She placed a stack of scrap paper beside it and watched the first visitor hesitate. He wrote something, folded it twice, and dropped it through the slot. Then he borrowed a book about mushrooms and left without saying a word to anyone.

By Friday, the box held seventeen questions. Some were practical: How can I keep basil alive? Others were less so: Do birds recognize individual clouds? One was written in blue crayon: Where does yesterday go when it is finished? Mara read them after closing, while the radiators clicked and the windows darkened. She resisted the temptation to sort the questions into sensible and foolish piles. A question, she thought, was already evidence of attention. That made it worth keeping, even if nobody knew how to respond, or whether a response was what its writer had wanted in the first place.

On Monday she pinned three questions to a corkboard near the entrance and added a note inviting responses. By lunch, someone had recommended a brighter windowsill and less water for the basil. A retired pilot wrote that clouds changed too quickly for him to recognize them reliably, though he could not speak for birds. Beneath the question about yesterday, a child drew a river carrying tiny calendars toward the sea. Nobody signed the drawing. Mara liked that best. It allowed the image to belong to everyone who stopped to look, including the person who had made it in the beginning.

The board grew. People contributed recipes, guesses, diagrams, and stories that wandered away from their subjects before returning by unexpected routes. A mechanic explained the sound a kettle makes before boiling. A teenager offered a list of songs for anyone who felt lonely on a bus. Someone asked why apologies were easier to compose in the shower. Someone else replied that water gave words a place to hide until they were ready. Mara could not verify the claim, but she noticed that the answer stayed on the board longer than almost all of the more confident explanations people had offered.

Not every exchange was gentle. A question about cutting down an old tree brought sharp replies from neighbors who had argued about it for years. The roots had broken a pavement; the branches shaded a bedroom; the tree held a nest each spring. For a day the board became a battlefield of underlining and exclamation marks. Then Mara added another sheet beneath the dispute: What would each person miss if they got exactly what they wanted? The answers did not settle anything. They did, however, become longer and a little harder to dismiss with a single impatient stroke of ink.

As winter approached, the railway station felt less abandoned than it had in years. People lingered by the board and discovered that the author of a useful answer might be standing beside them in a damp coat. Conversations began awkwardly, then found their own pace. A baker and a schoolteacher compared notes on patience. Two sisters who had not spoken for months met while reaching for the same pencil. They did not resolve their quarrel that afternoon. They did agree to have tea. In a town accustomed to measuring change by construction projects and election results, this progress went unrecorded.

In January, the roof began to leak. Buckets appeared between the history shelves, and the council announced that repairs would require the library to close for several weeks. Mara worried about the people who depended on the building, especially those who had nowhere else to sit without buying something. Before she could make a plan, a question appeared in the box: Where can we put the library while the library is away? Answers arrived quickly. The bakery offered a table. The church offered a room. A bus driver offered an empty vehicle on its afternoon break, though nobody accepted that.

For a month, the library scattered across town. Books traveled in crates, and the question board moved to the bakery window. The arrangement was imperfect. Flour dusted the covers, the church room was chilly, and nobody could remember where the gardening books had gone. Yet visitors found one another. A woman looking for a dictionary discovered the gardening books under a table and took one home instead. Later, she returned it with a packet of seeds taped inside a paper envelope. On the envelope she wrote: For the next person who needs something to begin before spring has actually arrived here.

When the station reopened, the clock above the entrance was running seven minutes slow. Mara meant to have it fixed, but other tasks intervened. People returned the crates, rehung the board, and claimed their favorite seats. The wooden box went back on the desk, looking slightly worn from its travels. Near closing time, Mara found a new question inside: How do you know when a place belongs to you? She considered writing an answer. Instead, she pinned the question up, switched on the lamp beneath it, and left a pencil ready for whoever came through the doors the next morning.

### The Repair Table

Every Saturday, a folding table appears outside the library in my neighborhood. It has a blue plastic cloth, a jar of mismatched screwdrivers, and a handwritten sign that says, “BRING YOUR BROKEN THINGS.” At first, I assumed it was a charity collection. Then I noticed a woman in a green coat taking apart a toaster while its owner watched, holding the loose crumb tray like a serving dish.

The table belongs to no shop or organization. It was started by a retired electrician named Luis, who got tired of seeing useful objects left beside the trash bins. He put a notice on the library bulletin board, borrowed the table, and showed up one Saturday with his tools. Three people came. One brought a lamp, one brought a radio, and one brought a cake.

The lamp needed a new plug. The radio could not be saved, though Luis kept it open for an hour, tracing wires with a magnifying glass. The cake, as it happened, needed nothing at all. Its maker had misunderstood the notice and thought the event was a neighborhood party. She stayed anyway, cutting slices with a pocketknife while Luis worked.

A year later, the repair table has a small crowd of regulars. There is Priya, who sews torn coats and replaces buttons. There is Ben, a teenager who can diagnose many computer problems but has not yet learned to arrive on time. There is Mrs. Chen, who specializes in umbrellas and says that most people open them too roughly. Nobody has found a polite way to disagree with her.

I began stopping by because my apartment is on the way to the library, and because watching someone solve a problem is a pleasant form of rest. The work is usually slow. There are screws to sort, parts to inspect, and long pauses while somebody searches for the right word. Sometimes a repairer simply looks at an object from every angle, turning it over in their hands.

One morning, a boy brought in a toy train that had stopped moving. It was bright red, with a smiling face painted on the front, and he placed it on the table with great care. Ben opened the battery compartment and found a spring bent flat. He lifted it gently with a screwdriver, inserted fresh batteries, and set the train on the pavement. It moved about two feet before striking a crack.

The boy cheered. His mother thanked Ben, then asked what she owed him. Ben pointed to the jar beside the sign, which contained a few coins, two safety pins, and an orange button. She put in five dollars. The boy asked if he could have the button, and after some discussion, his mother exchanged it for a coin from her purse.

Not everything ends so neatly. A man once brought a coffee grinder that had belonged to his father. Its motor had burned out, and the replacement part was no longer made. Luis searched online for a while, then explained the problem. The man nodded, but did not take the grinder back immediately. He asked whether the motor might still be useful to someone, even if it would never run again.

Luis said he could keep the cord and the little rubber feet. The rest would probably have to go to an electronics recycling depot. The man considered this, then asked for a screwdriver. He removed the rubber feet himself and put them in his coat pocket. He left the grinder with Luis and walked away carrying only its glass jar, which he said he might use for screws.

The table has changed my sense of what a broken thing is. I used to imagine an object passing abruptly from useful to useless: a switch clicks, nothing happens, and the object becomes trash. At the table, that moment stretches out. A failure might be caused by a dirty contact, a loose wire, or a part that costs less than a bus ticket. Sometimes the cause remains a mystery.

There are practical reasons to be cautious about this way of thinking. Repairs take time, tools, and knowledge. A cheap replacement can cost less than an afternoon of skilled work, and some objects are sealed so tightly that opening them causes further damage. The volunteers do not pretend otherwise. They often tell people to buy a replacement, especially when an electrical item seems unsafe.

Still, they are willing to look first. That willingness draws people who have nowhere else to take a wobbly chair or a jacket with a broken zipper. It also draws people with questions. A woman who came for a lamp repair returned the next week to learn how to replace a plug. She practiced on an old cord, under Luis’s supervision, and took notes on an envelope.

By the time winter arrived, the library offered the group a corner indoors. The volunteers were reluctant to lose their spot by the entrance, where passersby could see them, but the first cold morning settled the matter. They carried the table inside and set it up between the returns desk and a shelf of travel guides. Mrs. Chen brought a small rug to catch the water dripping from umbrellas.

On the last Saturday before the holidays, the table was crowded. Priya worked on a child’s coat while the child sat nearby drawing a map of a kingdom made entirely of stairs. Ben was late, but arrived carrying a box of cables he had sorted by size. Luis had brought a thermos of coffee, and the cake maker appeared again with a tin of cookies. This time she knew what the gathering was.

As I left, I saw the boy with the red train coming through the door. He was older by several inches and carried the train under one arm. I wondered if it had broken again, but he set it on the rug and switched it on. It ran past the legs of the table, slowed at the edge, and stopped. He picked it up, turned it around, and sent it back the other way.

Every neighborhood has a machine for keeping time, though it rarely looks like a clock. In one place it is the bakery that turns on its lights before dawn. In another it is the bus that sighs at the corner every twenty minutes, or the dog that announces the mail carrier with an indignation renewed each morning. These small repetitions tell people where they are in the day. They also make a place feel inhabited, not simply by individuals, but by habits shared among strangers.

I like to imagine a neighborhood built around a library of things. It would lend books, certainly, but also ladders, sewing machines, cake pans, folding chairs, and the kind of enormous cooking pot that seems necessary exactly once every three years. The building would be modest, perhaps a former shop with wide windows and a stubborn front door. Its shelves would contain objects waiting patiently for their next brief importance. A person could enter looking for a drill and leave with the means to hang a shelf, repair a chair, and feed twelve people.

The most useful items would probably be unglamorous. Extension cords would disappear quickly before summer parties. A sturdy cart would be popular among people moving apartments. Someone would always need a pair of pruning shears, and someone else would return them with an apology for being a day late and a small branch of rosemary as thanks. The library would develop a practical knowledge of local life: when gardens wake up, when school projects are due, and when everyone suddenly remembers that windows need washing.

Naturally, things would break. A tent would come back with a bent pole. A blender would make a noise like a gravel truck and then stop. At first, these failures might seem like evidence that sharing is impractical. Yet every broken object would also present a choice. Throw it away, pay someone to repair it, or learn enough to attempt the repair together. The library could hold a monthly repair evening, with mismatched chairs, a kettle, and a table covered in screws. Some objects would survive. Others would provide useful lessons before departing.

There would be arguments, too. A ladder reserved for Saturday would not be returned until Monday. Someone would insist that a coffee grinder had been cleaner when they borrowed it. The rules would grow slowly from these disagreements: how long an item may be borrowed, what counts as ordinary wear, whether a person who loses a detachable part should pay for the whole machine. A good set of rules would not eliminate friction. It would give people a fair way to deal with friction without needing to become enemies.

Over time, the catalogue would become a history of local enthusiasms. A bread maker donated during a baking craze would sit beside a stack of gardening books, a projector once used for outdoor movies, and six identical pasta machines acquired through mysterious coincidence. Some items would prove unexpectedly popular. Others would remain almost untouched, their promise brighter than their usefulness. The staff might organize a shelf of forgotten equipment and invite people to borrow something unfamiliar, provided they could think of a plausible use.

The library would change how people imagined ownership. Not everything needs to sit in a cupboard waiting for its annual moment. A neighborhood of two thousand people probably does not need two thousand wallpaper steamers. Yet the purpose would not be to make private possessions seem shameful. A beloved bicycle, a grandmother’s mixing bowl, or a worn set of woodworking tools can carry a history that no shared catalogue could replace. The point would be to distinguish between things we treasure and things we merely store.

There would be quieter benefits as well. A newcomer might ask how to use a sewing machine and discover that the person checking it out knows a good tailor, a decent dentist, and a walking route that avoids the busiest road. An older resident might borrow a cart and find someone willing to help lift it down the steps. None of these encounters would have to become a friendship. There is value, too, in recognizing another face at the market and knowing that a small exchange has already gone well.

I suspect children would understand the place quickly. They are accustomed to borrowing, trading, and learning the unwritten rules of communal objects. They would be fascinated by the unusual equipment: the telescope with its many knobs, the carpet cleaner shaped like a tiny vehicle, the metal detector that promises buried treasure and usually finds bottle caps. A child who borrows a telescope might see the moon in detail for the first time. Another might lose interest after ten minutes. Both could return it for someone else to try.

The library would not solve loneliness, waste, or inequality on its own. It would require money, maintenance, good management, and people willing to contribute more than they take when they can. Some neighborhoods would need safer housing or reliable buses far more urgently than a collection of shared tools. But a small institution can still matter. She looked at the coffee. “And the elevator?”

“Inspection expires tonight.”

“So it gets a week off.”

He smiled. “I suppose it does.”

He handed her an envelope. Inside was the severance agreement, which she had already signed, and a card with everyone’s names in it. Some had added short messages: *Thanks for always holding the door.* *Best of luck.* The man from the third-floor insurance office had drawn a little elevator with a smile on it.

“You should write your number down for us,” the manager said. “In case there’s a reunion.”

“Of the building?”

“Of the people.”

She took out the business card and wrote her number on the back. The manager put it carefully in his wallet, behind a photograph of a dog.

At closing time she rode up to the roof. There was no button for it; she had to use the key. The elevator hesitated between floors, then rose the final few feet.

From the roof she could see the train tracks, the river, and the new apartment building that had blocked the sunset from the west-facing offices. Below, the ficus man was trying to fit the enormous leaf into the back of a hatchback. He rearranged it three times. On the fourth attempt, the leaf snapped off.

He stood holding it for a moment. Then he set it gently on the passenger seat and closed the door.

Mara stayed until the light changed. She had nowhere particular to be, although her cat would soon begin making a persuasive case for dinner.

When she returned to the elevator, she found that she had left the door open. The car waited where she had stopped it, warm from the afternoon sun. She stepped inside, turned the key, and pressed the button for the ground floor.

It stopped at seven.

“Fine,” she said, and waited for the doors to close.

It stopped at six, and five. At four, she stepped out into the dark corridor. She took the little flashlight from her bag and aimed it at the water stain. The horse’s head had grown; damp had spread down the wall in a shape that might have been a neck.

She took a photograph. Then she went back to the elevator and let it finish its slow descent.

On the first Tuesday of every month, the town lost eleven minutes.

Nobody knew where they went. At 3:14 in the afternoon, the church clock struck once, and then it was 3:25. Bread burned. Conversations acquired strange gaps. A woman once found herself holding a small green frog in the post office, with no memory of how either of them had arrived.

The town council formed a committee, which met for seven years and produced a report recommending further meetings.

Most people learned to live with it. Shopkeepers turned off their ovens at three. The school let children out early. Lovers avoided making promises on Tuesdays.

Then, one autumn, a boy named Elias decided to stay awake.

This was not, as his mother pointed out, a plan. Everyone stayed awake during the missing minutes. That was part of the mystery.

“I mean properly awake,” Elias said.

He prepared by drinking three cups of tea and tying a bell to his wrist. At 3:13, he sat beneath the church clock with a notebook on his knees.

At 3:14, the bell rang.

At 3:25, he was still there, but his notebook was open to a page he had not written on.

**BEHIND THE CLOCK**, it said, in his handwriting. **BRING SOMETHING BROKEN.**

Elias had a toy boat with a cracked hull. He had kept it under his bed since he was six, though he no longer remembered why it mattered. He put it in his coat pocket and waited a month.

The next Tuesday, at 3:13, he climbed the narrow stairs inside the church tower. Behind the clock face was a little door he had never noticed, painted the same color as the wall.

At 3:14, it opened.

On the other side was a workshop lit by hundreds of small lamps. Its shelves held chipped cups, snapped violin strings, torn letters, watches without hands. At a long table sat an old woman in a blue apron, carefully mending a paper crown.

“You’re early,” she said.

“I thought I was late.”

“That too. What did you bring?”

Elias showed her the boat. She took it, ran her thumb along the crack, and nodded.

“A good one. Sit down.”

He sat. Outside the workshop window, the town was perfectly still. A pigeon hung above the square, one wing lifted. A man had stopped halfway through sneezing.

“What is this place?” Elias asked.

“The time people put aside when they can’t bear to throw a thing away.”

She reached for a brush and a pot of glue. On her worktable lay a photograph torn neatly in half. In one piece was a man beside a cake; in the other, a woman holding a knife to it. The old woman fitted the edges together.

“The town made this room,” she said. “Not all at once. A little each month. Enough time to mend what people couldn’t manage themselves.”

“Why don’t they remember coming here?”

“Some do. Most don’t need to.”

Elias watched her set the photograph aside and take up his boat. She pressed glue into the hull and bound it with a thin strip of cloth.

“My father gave me that,” he said. “Before he went away.”

The woman glanced at him. “Would you like it back when I’m finished?”

He hesitated. He had expected her to know what the crack meant, perhaps even how to fix the part of him that still waited for the front door to open.

“Yes,” he said.

She handed him another brush. “Then help me hold this.”

Together they worked until the hull was sound. The woman filled a basin and floated the boat in it. Water rose around the red paint, but none came through.

A bell sounded somewhere overhead.

Elias hurried down from the tower with the boat tucked under his arm. In the square, the pigeon landed, and the man finished sneezing.

At home, Elias put the boat on his windowsill. A few days later, he found a tin of red paint in the shed and touched up its bow.

The following month, the town lost eleven minutes as usual. At 3:25, the baker returned to her shop carrying a plate she had glued back together. It had belonged to her sister. She set it on the counter, then wrote her sister a letter and went out to post it.

The town’s smallest museum occupied a room above the bakery, and for forty-three years its only exhibit was a chair.

The chair was not particularly old. It had no royal associations, no remarkable carvings, and no clear reason to be displayed behind a velvet rope. It was a kitchen chair, painted blue, with a shallow groove in the seat where someone had once set down a hot pan.

Visitors came up the stairs because the sign outside said MUSEUM, and because the smell of bread made them feel generous toward whatever lay beyond it. They would stand before the chair for a minute or two, read the label, and leave.

The label said:

**CHAIR, BLUE**

**Unknown maker, approximately 1950**

**Please do not sit.**

When Mara inherited the museum from her aunt, she thought there must be more to the story. Her aunt had been the kind of person who kept receipts in labeled tins and wrote the date on every jar of jam. Surely she had not spent half her life guarding an ordinary chair for no reason.

Mara searched the room. She found the visitor books, a broken fan, three pencils worn almost to their ferrules, and a shoebox full of postcards from people who had once lived in the town. There was no file on the chair.

In the first visitor book, the earliest entry read: *Lovely chair. Best of luck.*

The next said: *A very blue experience.*

By the third year, the comments had become more earnest.

*My father had one like this.*

*I sat in the bakery downstairs and remembered my mother cutting an orange into quarters.*

*Thank you for keeping it.*

Mara took the books to the café across the square, where old Mr. Bell sat every afternoon with his tea.

“Did you know my aunt before the museum?” she asked.

“Of course.”

“Why did she open it?”

Mr. Bell considered this. “She had the room.”

“And the chair?”

“She had that too.”

Mara waited, but he stirred his tea.

At the bakery, she asked Mrs. Patel, who had worked there since she was sixteen. Mrs. Patel wiped flour from her hands and looked up at the ceiling.

“Your aunt started bringing the chair downstairs after your uncle died,” she said. “She’d put it by the window and sit in it while we closed up. Didn’t say much.”

“Was it his chair?”

“I think he fixed it once. One leg used to wobble.”

“Then why put it upstairs?”

Mrs. Patel smiled. “You’ll have to ask someone who was there when she did.”

Mara found him watering the flower boxes outside the pharmacy. Mr. Keane had been on the town council when the museum opened. He remembered the meeting because his wife had been annoyed he missed their anniversary dinner.

“Your aunt came to us with a petition,” he said. “She wanted a grant for a museum.”

“Of a chair?”

“She didn’t mention that part. She said we needed somewhere for people to come in from the rain.”

The council had refused the grant, but her aunt opened the museum anyway. She painted the sign herself and borrowed the velvet rope from the town hall. When the council asked for it back, she sent them a bill for the paint she had spilled on her coat at their Christmas party. They let her keep the rope.

That evening Mara went upstairs and sat on the forbidden chair. It was sturdy and comfortable enough. Through the window she could see the square, the pharmacy, and Mr. Bell making his slow way home.

She stayed until the bakery closed.

Over the next week, she tried to improve the museum. She washed the window, replaced the dead bulb, and wrote a new label about her aunt. Then she read it back and took it down. It described a woman with a coat, a paintbrush, and a talent for getting her own way. None of it explained why people had returned year after year to look at the chair.

On Saturday, a man arrived carrying a yellow plastic bag. He was perhaps seventy and wore a suit that had seen better days.

“I was hoping this was still here,” he said.

He looked at the chair for a long time. Mara stayed at the desk, pretending to sort postcards.

“My wife came up once,” he said at last. “Years ago. She told me about it when she got home.”

Mara asked what his wife had said.

“She said there was a chair in a museum. I thought there must be more to it, but that was all she told me.”

He put the bag on the floor.

“She died in March. I’ve been meaning to come and see it for myself.”

Mara moved the rope aside. “Would you like to sit down?”

The man looked at the label, then at her.

“It’s all right,” she said. “I’m in charge.”

He sat. From downstairs came the sound of trays being stacked and someone laughing at a joke they had heard before. The man rested his hands on his knees. After a while, he picked up his bag and thanked her.

The following morning, Mara made a new sign for the street. It still said MUSEUM, but underneath, in smaller letters, she added: **A chair upstairs. All welcome.**

She moved the velvet rope into the cupboard. Then she took a second chair from the bakery and placed it beside the first, facing the window.

When the rain began that afternoon, two people came in. One bought a loaf. The other climbed the stairs, shook out her umbrella, and asked Mara what there was to see.

Mara showed her.

The town kept its lost things in a room beneath the swimming pool.

Most were ordinary: goggles, towels, a single shoe that had been waiting so long its owner was surely old enough to vote. But behind a locked door, on shelves made damp by the pool above, were the things people didn’t know they had lost until someone handed them back.

A man once came in for his umbrella and left with the memory of his mother singing while she peeled potatoes. He sat on the curb outside for twenty minutes, holding the umbrella closed in the rain.

I worked there on Tuesdays.

My job was to label the items. This was harder than it sounds. Courage, for instance, came in many forms: a small brass button, a warm stone, a letter with no address. Patience was usually a spool of thread, though once it arrived as a sleeping moth.

The room had rules. We couldn’t advertise. We couldn’t keep anything for ourselves. And we couldn’t return an item unless its owner asked for it, even if they didn’t know quite what they were asking for.

“What am I looking for?” people would say.

“That depends,” I’d tell them. “What have you tried?”

One Tuesday, a girl came down the stairs carrying a paper bag. She was perhaps twelve, with wet hair and a swimming medal knocking against her zipper.

“I think you have something of mine,” she said.

“What is it?”

“I don’t know. My dad says I used to be funny.”

I asked her to wait. In the back room I found a jar full of laughter, a packet of riddles, and a wind-up duck that marched in circles. None had her name on it. On the bottom shelf, though, was a small red mitten. Its label read: **THE ABILITY TO BE SILLY WITHOUT FEELING WATCHED.**

“Is that it?” she asked when I brought it out.

“I think so.”

She put it on. It was too small, but she worked her fingers in anyway.

“Nothing’s happening.”

“Maybe you have to try it somewhere else.”

She looked disappointed, but she thanked me and left the medal on the counter by mistake. I ran upstairs after her and found her in the lobby, standing in front of the vending machine.

I held out the medal. She took it, then glanced at her reflection in the glass. Wearing one red mitten and one bare hand, she made the mitten wave at her.

She looked around to see if anyone was watching.

I pretended to examine the price of crisps.

After a moment, she made the mitten wave again, this time with its thumb tucked in, like a tiny person bowing. Then she laughed, just once, and went out to meet her father.

Downstairs, I wrote **RETURNED** on the label and put it in the empty jar.

The Department of Unfinished Things occupied the top floor of a building that had never been finished. The stairwell ended abruptly at the ninth floor, where someone had painted a door on the wall and, after several years, installed one.

Mara worked at the intake desk.

Most days, people brought her small things: scarves with six inches left to knit, letters that began *Dear Dad*, birdhouses without roofs. She gave each object a number and placed it on a shelf in the appropriate room. Once a month, if the owner hadn’t returned, the department sent a reminder by post.

The reminders rarely worked.

One rainy Tuesday, a man arrived carrying nothing.

“I’d like to report an unfinished conversation,” he said.

“Do you have a record of it?”

“No. It was forty years ago.”

Mara took out a form. “Who was it with?”

“My brother.”

“Is he living?”

The man shook his head.

She marked the box labeled *Other*.

“What was the conversation about?”

He considered this. “A bicycle.”

Mara looked up.

“He’d borrowed mine without asking. I was fourteen. I told him he was the worst brother in the world, and he said he didn’t care what I thought. Then he went outside, and our father called us in for dinner, and that was the end of it.”

“The end of the conversation?”

“The end of the argument, anyway. We spoke after that. Thousands of times.”

Mara waited.

“He died in March,” the man said. “Lately I keep remembering the bicycle. I suppose I’d like to know whether he really didn’t care.”

She put down her pen.

The department had a procedure for unfinished conversations. It required both parties to attend a meeting, at which a clerk would read the original transcript aloud. They could then continue, amend, or formally abandon the exchange. Mara had never processed a case involving a dead person.

“I’m sorry,” she said. “I don’t think we can retrieve the answer.”

The man nodded as if he had expected this. “Could you at least file the question?”

She almost told him no. The shelves were full, and the director had sent three memoranda that month about capacity. But the man stood patiently, his raincoat dripping on the floor, and Mara had a spare envelope in her drawer.

She wrote *Did you care what I thought?* on a slip of paper, sealed it, and gave him a receipt.

That evening, while putting it away, she noticed that the envelope was heavier than it should have been. Inside was another slip of paper, folded so tightly it had the shape of a seed.

She unfolded it.

*Of course I did,* it said. *You were my big brother.*

Mara sat down. After a while, she checked the handwriting against the intake form. It was not the man’s. She checked her own, though she knew it wasn’t hers, either.

The next morning, she telephoned him.

“I have something for you,” she said.

He came in before lunch. She handed him the slip, and he read it twice.

“That sounds like him,” he said.

Mara told him she couldn’t explain where it had come from.

“I can,” he said. “I think I put it there.”

He explained that while she was filling out the form, he’d found a piece of paper in his pocket and written the reply himself. He had slipped it into the envelope when she turned to fetch the receipt.

“I wanted to see if it would feel different coming from someone else.”

“Did it?”

He looked at the little slip in his hand. “For a second.”

Mara felt foolish, then irritated. “You could have told me.”

“Yes,” he said. “I’m sorry.”

She took the file from his hands and reached for the stamp that said *CLOSED*.

“Wait,” he said.

He asked if he could take the question home. She opened the envelope and gave it to him. He folded the two slips together and put them in his wallet, beside a photograph of two boys standing with a bicycle between them.

After he left, Mara stamped the empty envelope *RETURNED TO OWNER*.

The first thing Mara found in the wall was a teaspoon.

It lay in the dust beneath the plaster, its handle bent into the shape of a question mark. She assumed a builder had dropped it there years ago, until she found the marble, the red mitten, and an envelope addressed in her mother’s handwriting to someone named *Tomorrow*.

Mara sat back on her heels.

She had come to the house to make it ready for sale. Her mother had been dead for three months, and the rooms still seemed organized around the expectation of her return: a cardigan on the kitchen chair, a grocery list held to the refrigerator with a magnet shaped like a pear. Mara had made steady progress through the cupboards, but the loose plaster in the hallway had turned an afternoon’s work into something else.

She opened the envelope.

Inside was a slip of paper.

*Ask Mara about the bird.*

That was all. No date, no explanation. Mara turned it over, hoping for more, but the back was blank.

She took the paper into the kitchen and looked at it while the kettle boiled. Her mother had always left herself notes: *Call dentist*, *Beans soaking*, *Don’t forget Jan’s birthday again*. Yet Mara could not remember her ever asking about a bird.

She called her brother.

“Did Mum ever tell you about something she put in the hallway wall?”

“Was it money?”

“No.”

“Then no.”

“There’s a note in there about a bird.”

He was quiet for a moment. “You had a bird.”

“I did?”

“Not properly. It flew into the kitchen window. You made a box for it.”

Mara looked out at the kitchen window. The glass had been replaced years ago; she remembered that much.

“What happened to it?”

“I don’t know. You wouldn’t let me near it.”

After the call, she carried her tea back to the hallway. She crouched beside the opening and reached inside. Her fingers found a smooth wooden button, a pencil worn down to a stub, and a photograph of her and her brother standing in the garden. They were children in the picture. Mara held a shoebox against her chest, and both of them looked fiercely at the camera.

The box had holes punched in its lid.

That evening she called her brother again.

“I found a photograph. You were there.”

“I told you I was there.”

“You said I wouldn’t let you near it.”

“I think that’s why I remember.”

Together they pieced it out. The bird had been a thrush, or perhaps a starling. Mara had lined the box with one of their father’s socks. Their mother had telephoned a wildlife rescue, then driven them all there with the box on Mara’s lap.

“And?” Mara said.

“And what?”

“Did the bird live?”

“I don’t know.”

Mara almost said that surely their mother would have known, but she could picture her now, standing at the kitchen counter and writing the note. She must have meant to ask the next time they spoke. Perhaps Mara had mentioned the bird in passing, years after it happened, and her mother had wanted to hear the rest of the story.

Mara looked again at the photograph. Her brother’s arm was reaching across behind her, his hand resting on the bottom of the box. She had not noticed it at first.

“I think you helped me carry it,” she said.

“Of course I did.”

She put the photograph and the note on the mantelpiece. The other things went into a tin for her brother to look through when he came on Saturday. He might remember the red mitten, too, or know why anyone had bent a perfectly good spoon.

Every Tuesday, the town put its unwanted things on the curb.

There were chairs with one short leg, lamps with no shades, boxes of books swollen by the damp. Children took turns testing discarded mattresses until a parent called them in. By nightfall, the useful things had usually vanished.

One Tuesday in October, a piano appeared outside number 14.

It was upright and black, though its finish had gone cloudy. A sheet of paper taped to the front said **FREE**, and beneath that, in smaller letters, **Still plays, mostly**.

The piano remained through Wednesday. On Thursday morning, someone added a second note: **We can help you load it.**

On Friday, the rain began. A man from number 14 came out and draped a blue tarpaulin over the piano, fastening it with a length of clothesline. He stood back to inspect his work, then went inside.

The woman across the street watched from her kitchen. Her name was Mara, and she had stopped teaching piano twelve years earlier, after the school had replaced its music room with an office. She still played at home, though not much. Her own piano had three keys that stuck in humid weather, and she had grown accustomed to leaving them out.

On Saturday, she crossed the street and rang the bell.

The man who answered was younger than she had expected. He wore an apron and had flour on one wrist.

“Is the piano yours?” she asked.

“It was my mother’s.”

“Is she moving?”

“She died in August.”

Mara apologized. The man looked down at his apron as though he had forgotten he was wearing it.

“I’m clearing the house,” he said. “I thought someone might want it.”

“May I try it?”

He untied the clothesline. Beneath the tarpaulin, the piano smelled faintly of furniture polish. Mara sat on the bench, which had been tucked underneath, and pressed middle C. The note sounded thin but true. She played a scale. Near the top, two keys made no sound at all.

“It needs work,” the man said.

“So do most things.”

She played a little more: the beginning of a piece she used to assign her students. Her fingers remembered the notes, but she stopped when she reached the broken keys.

“My mother played that,” he said.

“It’s a common exercise.”

“She played it badly.”

Mara smiled.

“She practiced every evening for about three months. I was sixteen. It drove me mad.” He leaned against the garden wall. “I’d forgotten until just now.”

“Did she give it up?”

“I suppose so. Or perhaps I got used to it.”

They stood looking at the piano. A bus passed, and the loose edge of the tarpaulin lifted in its wake.

Mara did not need another piano. Her front room was small, and she was saving for repairs to the roof. But she asked the man what he would do if nobody took it.

“Call the council, I suppose.”

She imagined the piano tipped into the back of a truck, the keys sounding one last accidental chord. She also imagined the bill for moving it, and the difficulty of getting it through her own front door.

“There’s a woman on Birch Street,” she said. “She restores old instruments. I don’t know if she buys them, but I could ask.”

The man brought out his phone. Mara gave him the woman’s number, then helped him pull the tarpaulin back over the piano. As they tied it down, he asked whether she still taught.

“Not for years.”

“My daughter wants lessons. She’s eight. We bought her a keyboard, but she only plays the demo songs.”

Mara tightened a knot. “That may pass.”

“Would you consider teaching her?”

She nearly said no. Her lesson books were packed in the attic, and she could not remember how to explain a time signature to a child. But the man was waiting, and she found she wanted to meet his daughter.

“She could come round next week,” Mara said. “We’ll see how it goes.”

That evening, she opened her piano and played the exercise again. At the stuck keys she stopped, pressed them firmly, and waited for them to rise. Then she began once more, slowly enough to give each one time.

The town’s lost-and-found was in the basement of the library, between the boiler and a room full of chairs nobody trusted.

Most people came for umbrellas. The umbrellas were sorted into three barrels: black, bright, and broken. If yours was black, the librarian would offer you a chair and suggest you cancel your afternoon.

I started working there in November, after the previous clerk retired. On my first day, she handed me a ring of keys and a notebook.

“Write down everything people leave,” she said.

The notebook began in 1974. Its early pages listed gloves, spectacles, a trombone mute, and “one jar, contents uncertain.” Later entries became stranger.

A Tuesday afternoon.  
The smell of a father’s coat.  
A woman’s ability to sing in front of others.

I asked the librarian about these.

“Oh,” she said. “Those go on the high shelf.”

The high shelf was empty.

I assumed this was a joke whose explanation had retired with the clerk. Still, when a man came in that Thursday and said he’d lost his temper, I opened the notebook.

“Where did you last have it?” I asked.

“At breakfast.”

“What does it look like?”

He considered. “Red, I suppose.”

I wrote down *red, approximately*. The man sat quietly while I searched the cupboards. After ten minutes, he said, “Actually, keep it if you find it,” and went upstairs.

In December, a girl came looking for a dog.

“Is it black, bright, or broken?” I asked.

“Brown. And old.”

I took her name and phone number and promised to call. She stood on tiptoe, looking past me into the room.

“Is that all of it?”

“There are more cupboards.”

“Can I see?”

The rules did not say children couldn’t search the cupboards. They didn’t say anything about children at all. I gave her a torch.

She inspected every shelf. Behind the encyclopedias, she found a wool mitten, a chess queen, and a photograph of a man holding a fish larger than his head. In the boiler room, she found a tin of biscuits from 1998. We agreed not to open it.

At the bottom of the last cupboard, she stopped.

“There he is.”

I saw only dust.

She crouched and held out her hand. “Come on, Pickle.”

Something moved against the hem of her coat. She smiled, the way people do when they’re trying not to cry in front of a stranger.

“He died last year,” she said.

I waited.

“Sometimes I can remember exactly how he felt. Today I couldn’t.”

She stroked the empty air once, twice, then stood up. “I’ve got him now.”

After she left, I climbed onto a chair and reached toward the high shelf. My fingers closed around something small and warm.

I brought it down carefully. In my palm lay a smooth green marble. I knew it at once: my brother and I had buried it beneath our apple tree when we were children, as treasure for whoever lived in the house after us. We had made a map and stained it with tea. I’d forgotten the marble, and the map, and how seriously we’d argued over where to dig.

The next morning I phoned my brother. He remembered the map. He also remembered that we’d dug the hole in the wrong garden and our neighbor had made us fill it in.

We talked for an hour.

After that, I kept a sturdier chair beside the high shelf. Most days I still sorted umbrellas. But when someone came down the stairs with an uncertain expression, I opened the notebook and asked what they were looking for.

The shop appeared between a laundromat and a locksmith on a Tuesday when Mara was already late.

Its window contained a single clock with no hands. Beneath it, a handwritten sign read:

**TIME RETURNED, WHEN POSSIBLE.**

Mara went inside because her train had been delayed and because, lately, she had been doing things for smaller reasons than that.

A woman sat behind the counter, sorting screws into a row of teacups.

“Do you sell clocks?” Mara asked.

“No,” said the woman. “We find time people have lost.”

Mara looked at the door. “I don’t think that’s possible.”

“It usually isn’t. What are you looking for?”

Mara thought of the three hours she had spent on hold with the insurance company. The year she had stayed in a job she disliked. The morning she had opened her phone in bed and somehow found herself eating lunch.

“Can you give me back a year?”

“Not all at once.” The woman pushed the teacups aside and brought out a small ledger. “We can look for a particular hour. They’re easier to identify.”

Mara had an answer before she knew she had been considering the question.

“The last time I saw my father.”

The woman uncapped a pen. “What happened?”

“I took him groceries. He made tea. I was in a hurry, so I drank it standing up.”

“Did you argue?”

“No.”

“Did he ask you to stay?”

“No. He knew I had things to do.”

The woman wrote this down. Then she went into the back room.

Mara could hear drawers opening, the scrape of a chair, the clink of something dropped into a dish. She looked around. There were no clocks besides the one in the window, though the walls were covered in pale circles where clocks might once have hung.

The woman returned carrying a paper bag.

“I found forty-three minutes,” she said. “It was an ordinary visit.”

“That’s the one.”

“You’ll have to spend them as they were. You can’t tell him what happened afterward, or ask him questions you didn’t ask.”

“Can I stay for the tea?”

“Yes. You won’t remember to hurry.”

The woman folded the top of the bag and handed it across the counter. It was warm, as if it had held bread.

Mara opened it.

Her father was in the kitchen, using the good knife to cut a tomato. He had already put the groceries away, except for a jar of mustard he was turning in his hands.

“This has seeds in it,” he said.

“You asked for mustard.”

“I know. I didn’t specify.” He put it in the cupboard. “How’s work?”

Mara told him about a printer that had broken at the worst possible moment. He listened and asked whether anyone had thought to turn it off and on again. She said several people had, with increasing force.

He made tea. They sat at the table while he ate his tomato sandwich. Outside, a neighbor was struggling to fit a rug into the back of a car. They watched her roll it tighter, then unroll it and try the other end.

“Could go and help,” her father said.

They waited a little longer, just to see. Then he put down his sandwich and went out.

The woman was sorting screws again.

“I thought there might be more to say,” Mara said.

“Was there?”

Mara folded the bag carefully. “I don’t think so.”

She paid, thanked the woman, and stepped outside. Her train was still delayed. She walked to the station slowly and called her mother from the platform.

“Nothing’s wrong,” Mara said when she answered. “I just wanted to know what you’re doing.”

Her mother was making soup, and for the next few minutes they discussed whether it needed more salt.

On the morning the sea went quiet, Mara was repairing a kettle.

Its whistle had been failing for months. It produced, instead of a shriek, a small embarrassed sigh. The owner, a man who wore his coat indoors, had asked her to make it sound as it had when his wife was alive.

“I can repair the whistle,” Mara had said. “I can’t promise the rest.”

Now she stood at her bench with the little brass fitting between her fingers. Through the open window she could see the water beyond the railway line, flat and blue as painted tin. It took her a while to notice what was wrong.

She looked up because she could hear the clock.

Normally, the sea covered the clock’s ticking, even here, three streets back from the shore. It covered conversations too, and dogs barking, and the groan of the early train. Mara had lived beside it for forty years and had never thought of it as loud. Only when it stopped did she understand how much it had been saying.

She went down to the beach. The waves were still coming in. They curled and broke around the stones, sending foam up toward her boots, but she heard nothing from them. A gull cried overhead. Somewhere a car door slammed.

At the waterline, a little boy was clapping at the sea, waiting for an answer.

Mara crouched beside him.

“Has it been like this long?” she asked.

He shrugged. “Since breakfast.”

His father stood a few yards away, holding a phone to his ear. “No,” he was saying, “I can see it moving. That’s what I’m telling you.”

By noon, the town had assembled at the shore. People took videos. Someone from the radio station came with a microphone and then seemed unsure what to do with it. A woman put her face in the water and came up laughing, though she wouldn’t say why.

Mara went back to her shop. On the way, she passed the bakery, where two customers were arguing over whether the silence had a cause. One blamed the shipping lanes. The other blamed the council.

She took a clean jar from her cupboard and carried it to the beach. She held it beneath a breaking wave, sealed it underwater, and brought it home.

The water inside sloshed when she tilted the jar. She could hear that. She set the jar on her bench and listened for a long time, but the water did nothing else.

That evening the man came for his kettle. Mara had forgotten it on the bench, its whistle still in pieces. She apologized and told him she would finish it in the morning.

He looked toward the shore. “I heard about that.”

“Have you been down?”

He shook his head. “I can hear the neighbors through the wall now. They play cards on Thursdays.” He paused. “I didn’t know.”

She offered him the loan of a kettle from the back room, but he said he had a saucepan.

The sea stayed quiet for six days.

People slept badly at first. Then they began to hear things they hadn’t before: the loose cover on a drain outside the post office, the harbor gate swinging in the wind, music from a house high on the hill. The man next door to Mara knocked on her wall one night to ask if she could hear his pipes. She could, and on Saturday she helped him fix them.

On the seventh morning, she woke before dawn to a slow, familiar rush. She sat up and listened. Another wave broke, and another.

She went to the window. In the dim light, she could just make out two figures on the beach. One bent down, perhaps to pick up a stone. The other waited beside them.

At nine, Mara opened the shop. The man arrived for his kettle and stood while she filled it and put it on the stove. When it boiled, the whistle came out clear and sharp. He smiled, then asked if she could make it a little quieter.

She adjusted it while he waited.

On the last Thursday before the bridge came down, the city sent a woman to record it.

Her name was Mara, and she worked in an office that usually recorded things nobody noticed until they stopped working: the warning bell at the reservoir, the hum of the old courthouse elevators, the tone played before announcements at the bus station.

“Why the bridge?” she asked her supervisor.

“It makes a noise,” he said.

Everything made a noise, but Mara had learned that this was not an argument worth having.

She arrived at nine with a microphone, a recorder, and a thermos of tea. The bridge crossed a narrow river that looked, from that height, like a strip of unpolished metal. Beyond it stood the new bridge: wider, brighter, and already carrying most of the traffic.

The old one creaked when the wind moved through its joints. It gave a low, hollow boom when a truck crossed. Each footstep set off a small chain of clicks beneath the pavement, like someone running a stick along a fence.

Mara was recording these when a man stopped beside her.

“Are you looking for the bird?” he asked.

“I’m recording the bridge.”

“Oh,” he said. “You’ll get the bird too, then.”

He was carrying a paper bag darkened at the bottom by grease. He set it on the railing and took out a pastry.

“What bird?” Mara asked.

The man pointed to a streetlamp halfway across the bridge. “There’s a starling that does the crossing signal.”

They waited. Traffic murmured from the new bridge. A cyclist passed behind them, and the old bridge clicked.

Then, from the streetlamp, came a clear mechanical chirp: *peep-peep, peep-peep.*

It was followed by a sound like a car alarm losing confidence.

“There,” the man said.

Mara turned the microphone toward the lamp. The bird performed the crossing signal twice more, then tried a few notes of something she couldn’t identify.

“My wife used to bring it crumbs,” the man said. “We’d walk over after her appointments.”

“At the hospital?”

He nodded. “She liked to stop here on the way back. Said she wanted to arrive home as a different person from the one who’d left.”

He broke a piece from the pastry and put it on the railing. The starling flew down, inspected it, and returned to the lamp.

“Not hungry,” he said. “Or doesn’t like lemon.”

They stood for a while. Mara watched the levels rise and fall on her recorder.

“Is your wife still in the hospital?” she asked.

“No. She died in February.”

“I’m sorry.”

He nodded, as if confirming a date in a diary. He brushed sugar from his fingers and picked up the paper bag.

Before leaving, he asked what would happen to the recording.

“It goes into the city archive,” Mara said. “People can request a copy.”

“Will anyone?”

“Sometimes they do.”

At the office, she listened through headphones. There was the groan of the girders, the truck’s boom, the long wash of tires on the new bridge. And there was the starling, reproducing the crossing signal so exactly that Mara glanced up from her desk, half expecting the little green figure to appear.

She filed the recording under *Infrastructure: Bridges, Eastbank*. Then she made a second copy and labeled it *Starling on bridge*. She put the man’s description in the notes, though she did not know his name.

Three weeks later, the bridge was gone. Mara took her lunch down to the river and sat where she could see the new one. It had smooth railings and lamps shaped like white teardrops. A cyclist crossed without making a sound she could hear.

She had nearly finished eating when a starling landed on the bench beside her.

It regarded her sandwich.

“Not hungry,” Mara told it.

The bird tilted its head. Then it made the long, flat beep of a reversing vehicle, and she laughed loudly enough that someone across the path turned around.

She tore off a bit of bread and set it on the bench. This time, the bird took it.

The first letter arrived on a Tuesday, addressed to the house that had been demolished three years earlier.

**To whoever lives there now,** it began. **There used to be a pear tree by the kitchen window. I wonder if it’s still there.**

The postman, who knew everyone on the street, carried it to the empty lot and looked through the fence. There was no tree. There was hardly anything: a mattress, a drift of wrappers, and the concrete steps that had once led to the front door.

He took the letter home.

This was not strictly allowed, but he had already opened it by mistake. His wife read it and said he should write back.

“What would I say?”

“The truth.”

So he did.

**The house is gone, I’m afraid. The pear tree too. The steps are still there.**

He signed his name and added, because it seemed unfriendly not to, **I’m sorry.**

A week later, another letter came.

**Dear Mr. Bell,**

**Thank you for telling me. My father planted the tree when I was born. He said that by the time I was old enough to remember anything, it would be old enough to remember me.**

**I don’t suppose you know what happened to the family who lived there last? Their name was Varga.**

Mr. Bell knew the Varga family. He had delivered birthday cards to their children, examination results, a parcel of Hungarian paprika that had split open in his bag. Mrs. Varga had once brought him a cup of tea while he was sheltering from a storm beneath her porch.

But he had not seen them since the house came down.

He wrote to say so, and the letters might have ended there. Instead, the woman wrote back with a small correction: the porch had been built by her father, and he had always insisted it was a veranda. She included a photograph of him standing on it in a suit too large for him.

Mr. Bell showed the photograph to his wife. She recognized the man at once. He had repaired their television in 1989 and refused payment because their first baby had just arrived.

Over the next few months, Mr. Bell and the woman exchanged what they knew. Her name was Clara. She had moved away at eighteen and now lived near the sea. Her father had died. Her mother had remarried. She remembered the yellow roses by the gate, which Mr. Bell did not, and he remembered a cat with one white ear, which she did.

One Saturday, Mr. Bell found Mrs. Varga’s youngest son working at the garden centre. He was thirty now, with a beard, but Mr. Bell recognized the gap between his front teeth. He asked after the family and then, cautiously, about the house.

“There was subsidence,” the son said. “We had to leave in a hurry. My mother was upset about the tree.”

“Did they cut it down?”

“No. She wouldn’t let them.”

Mr. Bell waited.

“We dug it up. It’s in her garden now, at the new place.”

That evening he sat at the kitchen table to write to Clara. He had spent several minutes trying to describe the size of the tree when he realized he did not know it. He phoned the garden centre, got the son’s number, and asked whether he might come and see.

Mrs. Varga welcomed him with tea. The pear tree was taller than the fence, its branches held up in places by wooden stakes. It had been a difficult move, she told him. For two years they thought it might die. Then, one spring, it flowered.

Mr. Bell took a photograph. Mrs. Varga picked three pears and put them in a paper bag for him to carry home.

He sent the photograph to Clara the next morning.

Her reply came on a postcard showing a grey sea.

**My father would have liked Mrs. Varga. Please thank her for me.**

At the bottom she had written: **I think he was right about the tree.**

In October, a small parcel arrived for Mr. Bell. Inside was a jar of pear jam and a note.

**From the tree’s first year in our garden,** Clara wrote. **My mother made more than we could eat. I found this jar at the back of her cupboard, and it seems only fair that you should have it.**

Mr. Bell was not sure how old the jam might be. His wife examined it, opened it, and pronounced it excellent.

They ate it on toast that Sunday, looking out at their own garden. The baby for whom the television had been repaired came by with two children of her own, and they finished the jar.

The town clock was seven minutes slow, which suited almost everyone.

The baker said it gave his bread a better chance. Schoolchildren preferred it because the first bell seemed to arrive reluctantly. Even the mayor, who had promised to fix it during three separate campaigns, admitted privately that the clock made him feel younger.

Only Mara objected.

She repaired watches in a shop beneath the clock tower, and every morning at eight she heard the great bell sound seven minutes after her own precise little clocks had chimed. She had written letters. She had offered her services for free. She had once climbed halfway up the tower with a toolbox before the caretaker found her and threatened to call the police.

Then one winter the caretaker died, and the mayor gave Mara the key.

The mechanism was older than she expected. Its iron teeth were worn smooth, its weights patched with lead. There was a nest behind the western dial containing three blue buttons and the bones of something small.

She found the problem quickly: a bent arm, easily straightened. But beside it lay a folded piece of paper, yellow and brittle. In an unsteady hand someone had written:

*Please leave it. He said he would be home at six.*

There was no name.

Mara sat on the dusty floor with the note in her lap. Outside, people crossed the square with their collars turned up. A delivery van stopped at the baker’s. A boy dropped a mitten, and a woman ran after him carrying it.

At six, the bell rang seven minutes late.

Mara folded the note and put it in her pocket. Then she straightened the arm.

The next morning, people were annoyed. Several missed the bus because they had come to trust the old clock’s lateness. The baker burned a tray of rolls, though he blamed the flour. The mayor took credit in a short speech that nobody attended.

Mara returned to her shop and opened the door. On the counter she placed a small glass dish containing three blue buttons. Customers sometimes asked where they had come from.

“The tower,” she said.

“Why were they there?”

“I don’t know.”

And when they asked about the clock, she told them it had been an easy repair.

People brought the usual things: umbrellas, gloves, a single roller skate. They also brought things for which there were no forms.

A woman once left a jar on the counter. “My husband’s laugh,” she explained. “It disappeared sometime in March.”

The librarian, whose name was Ada, held the jar to her ear. There was a faint sound inside, like a spoon tapping the rim of a glass.

“We’ll do what we can,” Ada said.

She wrote *LAUGH, HUSBAND’S* on a label and put the jar on a shelf. The woman returned every Tuesday to ask about it. The laugh never grew any louder, but eventually she began staying after Ada went upstairs, sorting the unclaimed gloves into pairs.

There was a boy who had lost the feeling that summer would last forever. Ada found him a chair and a cup of tea. She could not find the feeling, but she did find a photograph someone had left between the pages of an atlas: three children standing in a sprinkler, all of them blurry except for their feet. “That’s not what I mean.”

The town decided to save its sounds in the same year it stopped repairing the clock.

The clock stood over the old post office, and for forty years it had announced each hour with a noise like a spoon being dropped down a staircase. Then one Tuesday it struck eleven at breakfast, nineteen at lunch, and was gently disconnected.

People complained for a while. Then they complained about other things.

The sound project was Nora’s idea. She worked at the library and had noticed that people asked for recordings of things they could no longer hear: the old ferry horn, the rain on the tin roof of the school, the particular rattle of the number six bus.

She put a notice in the window:

**SOUNDS WANTED. NOTHING TOO SMALL.**

Mr. Patel brought a recording of his mother laughing, though he warned Nora that it included a pressure cooker whistling and someone saying a word he would rather she didn’t write down.

A child brought the squeak of his new shoes. His older sister brought the silence that followed after he took them off.

The bakery contributed the clatter of trays at four in the morning. The butcher sent in the bell over his door. Someone recorded the river from the bridge, and someone else recorded it from underneath, where it sounded like an entirely different river.

Nora catalogued everything. She wrote descriptions on index cards and kept the recordings on a computer behind the desk. On Thursdays, people could come in, put on headphones, and listen.

At first, most of them chose the grand sounds: the storm that flooded Market Street, the final whistle of the championship match, the fireworks from the summer the mayor’s hat caught fire.

Then people began to ask for stranger things.

“Do you have the gate at the allotments?” a woman asked. “Before they oiled it.”

“Have you got someone turning the pages of the newspaper?”

“Is there a kettle that sounds nearly boiled but isn’t?”

Nora learned that the things people missed were not always things they had liked.

One afternoon, the man who had disconnected the clock came into the library carrying a small recorder.

“I found this in a drawer,” he said. “Thought you might want it.”

It was the clock on the day it went wrong. In the recording, it struck eleven, paused as if considering its options, and struck eight more times. Beneath the clanging, someone in the street said, “Oh, for heaven’s sake.”

Nora laughed. The man did too.

She made a card for it: **POST OFFICE CLOCK, LAST DAY. WITH COMMENTARY.**

That Thursday, she put the recording on the library’s public speakers just before closing. People looked up from their books. A little boy began counting, lost his place, and started again.

When the last note had faded, the library was quiet for a moment. Then an elderly woman near the window said, “It was always two minutes slow.”

“It was not,” said the man beside her.

They argued about it all the way out. Nora held the door open so she could hear a little more.

When the ash tree died, the council sent a man named Ellis to remove it.

He arrived on a Tuesday with a saw, a thermos, and a sheet of yellow tape. An elderly woman was sitting on the bench, eating a pear.

“I’ll need the bench clear,” he told her.

She took another bite. “For how long?”

“An hour, maybe two.”

“That’s all right. I can go to the library.”

She stood, wiped her hands on a handkerchief, and walked away. Ellis put up the tape.

*If you find a key and don’t know what it opens, leave it here.*

There was no signature or date.

Ellis carried the box to the bench. He finished taking down the tree, loaded the branches onto his truck, and swept the path. Before leaving, he put the box beneath the bench, where it would be sheltered from rain.

“I found them in the tree.”

“Yes. I put them there.”

The clock above the bakery said 8:14. The one in the pharmacy window said 8:09. At the railway station, a great brass clock insisted it was nearly noon, although the shadows were still long and blue.

“You’ll want to use your own,” the stationmaster told her.

“My own what?”

“Clock.”

Mara looked at her phone. No signal, and the battery had died on the train.

The stationmaster nodded sympathetically. “Then you’ll want to ask someone.”

She had come to settle her uncle’s affairs. He had left her a small house, a modest debt, and a shop called LOST TIME, which she assumed was an antique store. The solicitor had given her a key and an address, but little else.

The shop stood between a florist and a place that repaired umbrellas. Its window was crowded with glass jars, each labeled in her uncle’s narrow handwriting.

*Seven minutes, Tuesday afternoon.*

*Forty seconds, waiting for a kettle.*

*One summer, approximately.*

Inside, the air smelled of dust and oranges. Shelves reached the ceiling. Behind the counter was a ledger, and beside it, a note.

*Mara,*

*I’m sorry about the debt. The shop may help with that. Please don’t open anything marked with a red dot.*

*Love,*

*Uncle Daniel*

Mara spent the morning sorting through invoices. At least she thought it was the morning. A woman came in carrying a jar wrapped in a tea towel.

“I’d like to sell this,” she said.

Mara unwrapped it. The jar held what looked like pale gray smoke.

“What is it?”

“My commute. Every morning for six years. I’ve retired now, and I don’t suppose I need it.”

“I’m not sure how much it’s worth.”

“Daniel gave my husband thirty pounds for his.”

Mara checked the till. There was enough cash, and the woman had the patient expression of someone accustomed to waiting for things. Mara paid her.

After the woman left, Mara opened the ledger. There were columns for purchase, sale, and provenance. Most entries were ordinary: dentist’s waiting rooms, delayed buses, meetings that had run over. Beside each was a price.

Near the back, Mara found a different sort of entry.

*Four minutes. Kitchen. Bought by Mr. Bell for his daughter.*

The price was much higher than the others.

That afternoon, a man in a paint-stained coat came in and asked for twenty minutes.

“What kind?” Mara asked.

“Something quiet. Somewhere warm, if possible.”

She showed him a jar labeled *Twenty-three minutes, conservatory, rain*. He held it to the light.

“I’ll take it.”

“What do you do with it?”

He glanced at her. “Daniel didn’t tell you?”

“He didn’t tell me much.”

The man turned the jar slowly in his hands. “My wife’s in the hospital. She sleeps most of the time. I sit with her, but she wakes up frightened, not knowing where she is. I thought this might give her somewhere pleasant to go.”

Mara sold him the jar. At the door he paused.

“Sorry about your uncle,” he said. “He used to deliver these himself when she was too ill to come in.”

That evening, Mara found a red-dotted jar on the highest shelf. Its label read: *Mara, age nine. Twelve minutes.*

She had not seen her uncle often after childhood. Her mother and Daniel had quarreled over something neither would explain. For years, birthday cards arrived without return addresses, then stopped. When Mara’s mother died, Daniel had sent flowers but had not come to the funeral.

She took down the jar.

Inside was a faint golden haze. She held it in her palm for a long time, wondering whether her uncle had kept it because it was valuable or because it was hers.

She opened it.

The shop disappeared.

She was sitting on a kitchen floor, cross-legged in pajamas. Rain tapped the window. Her uncle stood at the stove, trying to flip a pancake without a spatula.

“Watch carefully,” he said. “This is how professionals do it.”

The pancake folded over the edge of the pan and fell onto his slipper. Nine-year-old Mara laughed so hard she tipped sideways.

Her mother was there too, at the table with a cup of tea. Mara had forgotten that part. She was laughing, although she tried to hide it behind her hand.

Daniel picked up the pancake and bowed.

The memory ended. Mara was back in the shop, holding an empty jar.

On the morning the town’s clocks began running backward, Mara was late for work.

She noticed first in the kitchen. The second hand on the wall clock moved from twelve to eleven to ten. She tapped the glass. It continued. On her phone, the time read 7:43, then 7:42.

Outside, the baker was standing in his doorway, holding a tray of rolls.

“Did you see?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“Are we supposed to open?”

Mara looked down the street. The florist had put out her buckets of flowers. A bus passed with three passengers aboard, all staring at their phones.

“I would,” Mara said.

At the town hall, the clocks were going backward too, which was unfortunate because Mara’s job was to issue parking permits, and the permit software required a date and time. When she tried to enter one, the screen displayed an error message: **EXPIRATION CANNOT PRECEDE ISSUE.**

She called the software company. After a long wait, a man named Dennis answered.

“Have you tried restarting?” he asked.

“I’ve tried everything except going home.”

“Let me check with my supervisor.”

Mara put the phone on speaker and listened to a recording of a piano playing the same eight bars. Across the counter, an elderly woman waited for her permit, resting both hands on a walking stick.

“Would you like to sit?” Mara asked.

“No, thank you. I’ve been sitting all morning.”

They listened to the piano.

“My husband used to play,” the woman said. “Not well enough for recordings.”

“What did he play?”

“Mostly things he made up. He was very fond of one tune in particular. It went on so long you could leave the room, make tea, come back, and he’d still be playing it.”

“Was it good?”

“No,” said the woman. “But he was cheerful.”

Dennis returned to the line. His supervisor had recommended a full system reset.

“What happens to the permits we’ve already issued?” Mara asked.

“They should remain in the database.”

“Should?”

There was a pause. “Probably.”

Mara decided against the reset. She took a blank permit from the drawer, filled it out by hand, and stamped it with the town seal. The ink came out faintly purple.

“There,” she said.

The woman examined it. “Will it be valid?”

“If anyone asks, tell them I said so.”

The woman tucked the permit into her handbag and thanked her.

By noon—or what would ordinarily have been noon—the clocks were still running backward, but the town had settled into its day. The baker sold out of rolls. The bus completed its route. Children came home from school with worksheets explaining how the hands of a clock were *supposed* to move.

At four, Mara closed the permit office and walked home. The baker was sweeping flour from his step.

“Good day?” she asked.

“Not bad,” he said. “I opened.”

That evening, the clock on Mara’s kitchen wall stopped at 11:59. Its second hand rested there for a moment, then moved to twelve, one, two.

Mara watched it for a while. Then she set it to the right time and went to make dinner.
