The town had a department for everything.

There was a Department of Roads, which filled potholes; a Department of Trees, which planted trees and occasionally removed them; and a Department of Lost Things, which occupied a narrow office between the bakery and a shop that sold only lamps.

Most people assumed the Department of Lost Things dealt in umbrellas and keys. It did, but those were handled at the front desk. The more complicated losses were taken upstairs.

On her first day there, Mara found a small brown envelope on her desk. Inside was a slip of paper that read:

**ONE AFTERNOON, LATE SUMMER.  
LOST BY: MR. ELIAS VALE.  
LAST SEEN: APPROXIMATELY FORTY YEARS AGO.**

She took it to her supervisor.

“How do you lose an afternoon?”

“Gradually,” he said. “That’s why these are difficult.”

Mr. Vale arrived at eleven. He was a retired carpenter with hands that looked capable of repairing a chair without being asked. Mara offered him tea, which he declined, then accepted, then forgot to drink.

“What can you tell me about the afternoon?” she asked.

“It was hot.”

“Anything else?”

“My brother was there.”

Mara wrote this down.

“He died?”

“No. He lives in Bristol. We haven’t spoken in twenty-three years.”

“Do you remember why?”

Mr. Vale considered. “I remember several reasons. I’m not sure which one we used.”

Mara opened the filing cabinets. They contained things people had misplaced without knowing where to begin looking: the courage to apologize, a tune heard once through an open window, the exact color of a childhood bedroom. Some had been carefully labeled. Others had been dropped into drawers by previous employees who apparently meant to come back to them.

She searched under **A** for afternoon, **B** for brother, and **S** for summer. She found three picnics, a thunderstorm, and the smell of a dog named Pepper, but nothing belonging to Mr. Vale.

“I’m afraid I can’t locate it yet,” she said.

He nodded, as though this was what he had expected. At the door, he paused.

“There was a pear,” he said.

“A pear?”

“One of us had a pear. It was too hard to eat.”

When he had gone, Mara searched again. Under **P**, behind a folder marked *PARADES, DISAPPOINTING*, she found a small wooden box. Inside lay a pear, green and unripe. When she picked it up, she heard a faint sound: two boys laughing, and somewhere nearby, water moving over stones.

She phoned Mr. Vale. He came back the next morning.

Mara placed the pear on her desk. He touched it with one finger.

“We took it from Mrs. Barlow’s tree,” he said. “My brother climbed the wall, and I was supposed to catch it. I dropped it in the stream.”

“Do you remember the rest?”

“A little.” He picked up the pear. “He jumped in after it. He was furious with me. Then he slipped, and that made me laugh, which made him more furious.”

The pear softened in his hand. A dark bruise appeared on one side.

“He held it underwater,” Mr. Vale said. “Said if I wanted it, I’d have to come in too.”

He stood quietly for a while, holding the fruit. Mara made herself busy with the filing cabinet.

“Did you go in?” she asked at last.

“Yes. We stood in the stream and ate it together. It was awful.”

He laughed, and then, to his evident annoyance, began to cry. Mara handed him a box of tissues and continued looking through the cabinet until he was ready to speak.

“Can I take this?” he asked.

“Of course.”

A week later, a postcard arrived from Bristol. On the front was a photograph of a suspension bridge. On the back, in Mr. Vale’s careful handwriting, were four words:

**HE REMEMBERED IT TOO.**

Mara pinned the card above her desk. Then she opened the next envelope.

The first thing the sea gave back was a red shoe.

It appeared on the beach after a storm, upright in the sand, its laces neatly tied. No one paid it much attention. The sea gave back shoes all the time.

The next morning, there was a kitchen chair. On Wednesday, a brass key. On Thursday, seventeen blue marbles arranged in a circle around a dead jellyfish.

By Friday, people were walking the shore before breakfast.

They found a wedding ring, a bicycle bell, a saucepan with a dent in its side. A woman named Maeve found the green glass stopper from her mother’s perfume bottle, lost when she was seven. She knew it was the same one because she had scratched an M into the bottom with a pin.

The newspaper called it a mystery. The mayor called it an opportunity. By Saturday, someone had set up a coffee cart at the top of the beach and was charging three pounds for hot chocolate.

Maeve went down every morning with a canvas bag. She did not know what she was looking for, which made it easy to stay for hours.

Her mother had been dead for eleven years. The perfume stopper sat on Maeve’s kitchen table, catching the light. She had no bottle to put it in and could not remember what the perfume had smelled like. Still, she was pleased to have it.

On Tuesday, she found a postcard she had sent to her brother from Cornwall in 1998. It was addressed to a house he had not lived in for twenty years. The ink had faded, but she could make out her own handwriting:

*The weather is terrible. You would love it.*

Her brother had died the previous spring. He had been sixty-four and had called her every Sunday, even when he had nothing to say.

She sat on a rock with the postcard in her lap until the tide came in.

After that, she began to notice that people were leaving the beach quietly. They still arrived in groups, laughing and carrying buckets. But those who found something often walked home alone.

A boy discovered a plastic dinosaur with one leg missing and ran all the way up the hill to show his father. At the coffee cart, a man held a small silver spoon for several minutes, turning it over and over. Then he bought two hot chocolates and drank both.

The mayor proposed a display in the town hall. People could bring their finds, label them, and share their stories with visitors. A few objects arrived: a compass, a teacup, a pair of spectacles. Most did not.

Maeve kept the postcard on her mantelpiece. Sometimes she picked up the telephone on a Sunday before remembering she had no one to call. Once, she dialed her brother’s old number anyway. A stranger answered, and Maeve apologized and hung up.

By October, the crowds had thinned. The coffee cart closed. The objects were still coming in, but the weather had turned and the stories in the newspaper had moved on to other things.

One morning Maeve found a small wooden boat. It had a green hull and a white cabin, and one of its windows had been colored in with black pen. Her brother had made it for her when she was little. She remembered sailing it in the bathtub, then in the harbor, where the string had slipped from her hand.

She carried it home carefully. The paint was chipped, but the boat was otherwise sound. Her brother had always been good at making things.

That evening, she filled the sink and set it afloat. It listed slightly to one side. She found a coin in a drawer and placed it inside the cabin, and the boat settled level in the water.

For a while she watched it. Then she took out the coin, dried the boat, and put it on the shelf beside the perfume stopper.

On Sunday, she called a friend she had not spoken to in months. They talked about the rain, the price of heating, and a neighbor’s troublesome dog. When her friend asked about the things the sea had returned, Maeve described the boat.

“I remember it,” her friend said. “Didn’t your brother paint the window black because he’d lost the little pane?”

Maeve laughed. She had forgotten that.

They talked for another hour. Afterward, Maeve went to look at the boat again. She turned it in her hands, found the marks where the missing pane had once been glued, and put it back on the shelf.

The first thing the town lost was Thursday.

People woke on Friday with the peculiar feeling of having forgotten an appointment. The baker found a tray of rolls burned black in the oven, though he distinctly remembered putting them in on Wednesday evening. The schoolchildren had finished worksheets in handwriting that looked like their own, only neater. A woman discovered that her husband had painted the garden gate blue. He was as surprised as she was, and neither of them liked it.

At the town meeting, the mayor suggested that everyone simply adjust their calendars.

“Cross it out,” he said. “These things happen.”

“Do they?” asked the baker.

The mayor admitted that he couldn’t recall.

For a while, life continued. The butcher labeled his sausages with two expiration dates, just in case. A girl in the school wrote a poem about the missing day and won a prize, although there was some disagreement about when the prize had been awarded.

Then the town lost the color yellow.

It went first from the daffodils. People thought they had grown strangely pale until someone noticed the same thing had happened to the postboxes, the crossing signs, and Mrs. Bell’s canary. The bird sang as before, a small white shape in its cage.

A few people left. Most stayed. The town had good water, a library, and houses their grandparents had built. Besides, the roads out were steep.

The librarian, whose name was Ada, began keeping a record. She wrote everything down in a ledger: the missing Thursday, the yellow, the taste of salt, which disappeared in late autumn. She left a space after each entry for anything that might return.

One morning she came to open the library and found a man asleep on the steps. He wore a coat too thin for the weather and held a paper bag against his chest.

“Are you all right?” she asked.

“I think so,” he said, sitting up. “I’ve come a long way.”

“Would you like some tea?”

He looked relieved. “Very much.”

Inside, Ada put the kettle on. The man set his bag on the table and unfolded its top. From it he took a yellow marble.

Ada stared at it. She had nearly forgotten what yellow looked like.

“Where did you get that?”

“I found it in a ditch,” he said. “There were other things too.”

He tipped out the bag. A pinch of salt spilled across the table, followed by a child’s yellow mitten, a folded worksheet, and a small brass plate engraved with the word *THURSDAY*.

Ada touched the plate. It was cold.

“Can you bring it back?” she asked.

“I don’t know how. I thought it might belong to someone here.”

They carried the bag to the town hall. People gathered around the table, passing the mitten from hand to hand. The baker put a grain of salt on his tongue and began to laugh.

The mayor lifted the brass plate. “Shall we hang it somewhere?”

“On the calendar,” said a child.

So they did. The next morning was Thursday. The baker opened his shop, the children went to school, and the mayor spent several hours answering questions about a road repair he had apparently approved during the previous Thursday. By evening, the daffodils were yellow again, though the canary remained white for another week.

The man stayed in town a few days, helping people look for things that had gone missing before anyone thought to record them. They found a wedding ring behind a dresser, a pair of spectacles in a coat pocket, and, in the butcher’s cellar, six jars of excellent pickles.

At the end of the week, he came to the library to say goodbye.

Ada thanked him and offered to buy him a warmer coat.

“I’d like that,” he said. “And could I borrow a book for the road?”

She showed him the shelves. He chose a book about birds, and Ada wrote his name and the date on the card inside.

“When should I bring it back?” he asked.

“Whenever you can,” she said.

He put the book carefully in his new coat pocket and set off down the steep road. That evening Ada added his name to the ledger, under a heading of its own. She left plenty of space beneath it.

The first thing Mara noticed was that the moon had moved.

Not across the sky. It was still where it ought to be, above the roofs of the town. But someone had shifted it a little to the left, as you might straighten a picture on a wall.

She mentioned it to her brother at breakfast.

“It’s always been there,” he said, without looking up from his toast.

“Not there exactly.”

He took a bite, then leaned back to look through the window. “You’re right. It used to be behind the chimney.”

“Thank you.”

“Mind you, we’ve had the kitchen extended.”

Mara went outside.

At the bus stop, she found Mrs. Vale studying a map. Mrs. Vale had lived in the town for eighty-three years and had never before needed a map, so Mara stopped beside her.

“Has something happened?” she asked.

“I’m trying to find the post office.”

“It’s on Market Street.”

“Yes, but Market Street isn’t.”

Together, they looked at the map. Market Street ran neatly between the bakery and the old fountain. In the world before them, the bakery stood beside the fountain, with no street between.

“Perhaps they’ve closed it,” Mara said.

Mrs. Vale folded the map. “With all the buildings still on it?”

They walked to the bakery. The baker was out front, sweeping flour from the pavement.

“Where’s Market Street?” Mara asked.

He rested both hands on the broom. “Well, that’s the question, isn’t it? My sister lives there. I’ve been trying to call her, but the line’s busy.”

“Does the back of your shop still open onto it?”

“I haven’t tried.” He led them inside, through the warm kitchen, and unbolted the back door.

Beyond it was Market Street.

The street was sunny and full of people, though rain was falling at the front of the shop. A delivery van had stopped outside the post office. Someone had left a bicycle against the fountain—the other fountain, farther along, which Mara had forgotten existed.

The baker called to a woman crossing the street. She waved and came over.

“This is my sister,” he said.

His sister stepped into the kitchen. She had an envelope in her hand.

“I’ve been ringing you,” he told her.

“The telephone’s off the hook. I couldn’t find a pen, and I thought I’d left one by it.” She held up the envelope. “Have you got a stamp?”

They all went back out through the front. The sister stood under the bakery awning, watching the rain.

“You’ve got a fountain here too,” she said.

Nobody knew what to do, so the baker made tea. He put four cups on the counter, and Mrs. Vale went home for a tin of biscuits. When she returned, she brought two more neighbours who had been looking for Market Street.

By noon, people were passing through the bakery in both directions. The baker moved his trays to make room and began selling buns to those waiting for the rain to stop. His sister found a stamp in her coat pocket and went back to post her letter.

Mara stayed until the rush had passed. Then she took a bun outside and ate it beside the fountain. The rain had stopped, and the moon was visible again, pale against the afternoon sky.

She looked at it for a long time. From the pavement in front of the bakery, she couldn’t quite tell whether it had moved.

The town library closed on a Tuesday, which seemed to Mara an unnecessarily quiet day for a disaster.

The notice on the door said STRUCTURAL CONCERNS. Behind it, someone had taped a second notice: BOOK DROP CLOSED. PLEASE DO NOT LEAVE MATERIALS OUTSIDE.

By noon there were eleven books outside.

Mara counted them from the bus stop. Someone had stacked them beneath the narrow overhang: a cookbook, three mysteries, a children’s atlas, and a fat biography of a man who had apparently been important enough to require two volumes. Volume Two was missing.

The sky was the color of a dirty plate. Mara crossed the street and carried the books into the bakery next door.

“They’ll get wet,” she told the woman behind the counter.

“They’ll get flour on them here.”

“Is that worse?”

The woman considered. “Put them by the radiator.”

Mara bought a roll she didn’t want and sat near the window. She was supposed to be on her way to an appointment about her mother’s house, but the bus had left without her. She had seen it coming and stayed exactly where she was.

By one o’clock, there were seventeen books.

At two, a man brought in a cardboard box containing a chess set, four audiobooks, and a framed photograph of the library’s first director.

“Found these in the book drop,” he said.

“How did you get into the book drop?” asked the baker.

“I’m the one who emptied it.”

“Then why didn’t you take them home?”

The man looked around the bakery, at the books by the radiator and Mara with her uneaten roll.

“Thought I had.”

He introduced himself as Leon. He had worked at the library for thirty-two years and had retired last spring. He’d come to see the building for himself.

“It’s the back wall,” he said. “Been moving for years.”

“Moving where?” Mara asked.

“Away from the rest of it, mostly.”

He picked up the children’s atlas and opened it carefully. Several countries had been colored in with pencil.

“I should erase that,” he said.

“Do you still work there?” the baker asked.

“No.”

“Then leave it.”

Mara called the estate agent and said she wouldn’t make the appointment. The agent asked whether everything was all right. Mara looked at Leon, who had found a place in the window for the library director’s photograph, and at the books people kept bringing through the door.

“Not entirely,” she said.

The baker found a spare shelf in the storeroom. Leon made signs from the backs of pastry boxes: RETURNS and, after some thought, BORROW SOMETHING IF YOU LIKE. Mara wrote down the titles as people took them. Most gave their names; one little boy gave only his age and the name of his dog.

At closing time, the baker packed Mara’s roll in a paper bag. Leon asked if she could come back the next day.

“I don’t know anything about books,” Mara said.

“You knew to bring them in.”

The rain began as they stepped outside. Across the street, water ran down the library windows, making the notices difficult to read. A woman hurried up with a book under her coat. She stopped at the door, then turned toward them.

Leon waved her over.

The town had a lost-and-found, though almost nothing in it was ever claimed.

It occupied a narrow room behind the library, between the boiler and a cupboard full of obsolete tax forms. There were umbrellas, of course, and gloves, and a child’s red boot whose owner had presumably continued growing with inconvenient speed. There was also a jar labeled TEETH, which the librarian insisted was mostly acorns.

Mara took the job after her father died. It was three afternoons a week, and the work consisted largely of attaching tags to things and waiting for people who did not come.

On her first Tuesday, a man brought in a yellow kite.

“Found it in the cemetery,” he said. “Stuck in the yew by the south wall.”

Mara wrote *kite, yellow, one* on a tag.

“Do you want my name?” he asked.

“Only if you want to leave it.”

He considered this. “No,” he said.

The kite was handmade. Its frame was two thin sticks, and the yellow paper had been patched with clear tape. Along the tail, someone had tied strips of an old shirt. Mara hung it from a hook above the filing cabinet, where it turned slowly whenever the boiler started.

A month later, a girl of about twelve came to the counter and asked whether anyone had brought in a kite.

“Yellow?” Mara said.

The girl nodded.

Mara fetched it. The girl held the frame up to the light and touched one of the taped patches.

“Is it yours?” Mara asked.

“It was my brother’s.”

There was a pause in which Mara might have offered sympathy, but the girl was examining the kite so carefully that she seemed not to need anything said.

“Can you fix it?” she asked.

One of the sticks had snapped near the top. Mara brought out the tape. Together they made a splint from a wooden coffee stirrer, then wound tape around it until the break felt secure.

“Thank you,” the girl said. She tucked the kite under her arm and went out.

That afternoon Mara checked the tag. She had written the date and the place it was found, but nothing else. She wished she had asked the man his name.

The next Tuesday, she found him in the cemetery. She recognized his green coat before she saw his face. He was kneeling beside a grave with a hand trowel and a packet of seeds.

“I work at the library,” she said. “You brought in a kite.”

He stood, brushing dirt from his trousers. “Yes. Did somebody want it?”

“A girl came for it. She said it belonged to her brother.”

The man looked down at the packet in his hand.

“He was my son,” he said. “She’s my daughter.”

Mara waited.

“I thought if I took it home, she’d put it straight back in the tree.” He gave a small, embarrassed laugh. “I was hoping she’d ask for help instead.”

“She asked me to fix it.”

“Did you?”

“We used a coffee stirrer.”

He smiled at that, and Mara felt suddenly unsure whether she had helped him or interfered.

That evening, on her way home, she saw the girl and the man in the park. The kite was in the air, pulling hard against its string. The man held the spool while the girl ran backward, watching the sky. Once, the kite dipped behind the trees, and Mara thought it had gone. Then it climbed again, trailing its uneven tail.
